PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 3994/03) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON] of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was arrested on suspicion of armed robbery. On [DATE_TIME] the Gdańsk District Court remanded him in custody in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed several offences of armed robbery.

Later, several other persons were detained and charged in connection with the same investigation conducted by the Department of Organised Crime of the Gdańsk Regional Prosecutor's Office. In the course of the investigation, the applicant's detention was prolonged several times.

On [DATE_TIME] the Gdańsk Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's and his eight co-suspects' detention until [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Gdańsk Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until [DATE_TIME]. It relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged and the severity of the anticipated penalty. The Court of Appeal further held that the detention on remand was the only measure which could secure the proper conduct of the proceedings given the nature of the charges and the relations between the suspects, who had acted in an organised group. It also considered that the prolongation of detention was justified by the need to obtain DNA evidence in order to corroborate evidence previously obtained.

On [DATE_TIME] the prosecution filed a bill of indictment with the Gdańsk Regional Court. The applicant was charged with several dozen counts of armed robbery which had been committed in an organised armed criminal group. The bill of indictment listed 120 charges brought against 19 defendants, who were all detained on remand. The case file comprised 114 volumes. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant be kept in custody until [DATE_TIME]. In addition to the grounds previously invoked, it referred to the complexity of the case, the significant number of defendants and the number of witnesses to be heard in the trial.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal extended the applicant's detention until [DATE_TIME], relying on the same grounds as in its earlier decisions.

The trial began on [DATE_TIME]. However, as of [DATE_TIME] the reading out of the bill of indictment by the prosecution had still not been concluded. Initially, the trial court held three hearings per month.

During the hearing held on [DATE_TIME] the trial court ordered the removal of the applicant and two other defendants from the court room. They disrupted the trial by screaming when the prosecutor was reading the bill of indictment, notwithstanding a warning from the presiding judge. Similarly, during the hearings held on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the trial court ordered the applicant's removal on the ground that he had disrupted the trial.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant and his seven co-defendants be held in custody until [DATE_TIME]. It considered that the trial could be terminated by the last-mentioned date. In addition to the grounds previously invoked, the Court of Appeal found that the prolongation of detention was justified under Article 263 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the particular complexity of the case. It further observed that the delays in the trial were partly attributable to some of the defendants who had attempted to disrupt the proceedings and, consequently, had to be removed from the court room. The Court of Appeal instructed the trial court to hold more than 3 hearings per month. Furthermore, it held that no other preventive measure could secure the proper conduct of the trial. In that respect, the Court of Appeal observed that there was a reasonable risk that the applicant and other defendants might interfere with the proceedings, given the nature of the charges, the severity of the anticipated penalty and the fact that such attempts had been made in the course of the investigation.

On 27, [DATE_TIME] and 29 [DATE_TIME] the Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's requests for the presiding judge to withdraw.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's and his nine co-defendants' detention until [DATE_TIME]. In addition to the grounds previously relied on, it considered that the applicant's detention was justified under Article 258 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure since that provision established a presumption to the effect that the likelihood of a severe penalty being imposed on the applicant might induce him to obstruct the proceedings. It also noted that the prolongation of his detention was justified by the volume of evidence to be heard at the trial.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant and his 17 co-defendants be kept in custody until [DATE_TIME]. It held that the grounds invoked in its previous decisions were still valid.

On [DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME] the Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed the applicant's request for the judges and lay members of the trial court to withdraw. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant and seventeen of his co-defendants unsuccessfully challenged the judges and lay members of the trial court.

On [DATE_TIME] the trial court refused the applicant's request for dismissal of his legal-aid counsel. Similar requests were dismissed on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's and eighteen of his co-defendant's detention until [DATE_TIME], relying on the same grounds as given previously. In addition, it observed that the trial could not have been terminated due to obstructiveness on the part of the defendants who had filed numerous requests challenging the trial court. It also noted that the trial court had taken various procedural steps in order to accelerate the proceedings.

In its decision of [DATE_TIME] dismissing the applicant's appeal against the decision of [DATE_TIME] prolonging his detention, the Court of Appeal held that Article 258 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure established a presumption to the effect that the likelihood of a severe penalty being imposed on the applicant might induce him to obstruct the proceedings. It added that the risk of absconding or tampering with witnesses in the present case did not have to be supported by any concrete facts, but resulted from the above presumption. The Court of Appeal also observed that although the applicant and other defendants were free to make use of their procedural rights, the abuse of those rights undoubtedly led to delays in the trial.

On [DATE_TIME] a new legal-aid counsel was appointed for the applicant. The previous counsel was discharged by the trial court from his duties at his own request and following a number of complaints made by the applicant.

Subsequently, the Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention on several occasions. The relevant decisions were given on [DATE_TIME] (prolonging his detention until [DATE_TIME]), [DATE_TIME] (extending his detention until [DATE_TIME]), [DATE_TIME] (ordering his continued detention until [DATE_TIME]), [DATE_TIME] (prolonging his detention until [DATE_TIME]) and [DATE_TIME] (extending his detention until [DATE_TIME]). In all those decisions the Court of Appeal stated that the grounds previously given for the applicant's detention were still valid. It also stressed the exceptionally complex nature of the case.

In its decision on the applicant's detention of [DATE_TIME], the Court of Appeal observed that up to [DATE_TIME] the main reason for the delays during the trial was the obstructiveness of the defendants and the abuse of the rights of the defence. It also observed that the trial could be concluded by [DATE_TIME] provided that the Regional Court endeavoured to organise the trial efficiently.

On [DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the Gdańsk Regional Court dismissed as unfounded the applicant's requests for various members of the trial court to withdraw.

On [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the trial court dismissed the applicant's application for release on health grounds, relying on the report prepared by the experts from the Gdańsk Medical Academy. The applicant was diagnosed with a number of ailments, including a brain tumour. However the experts determined that he could remain and receive treatment in detention.

In its decision of [DATE_TIME] dismissing the applicant's appeal against the decision of [DATE_TIME] prolonging his detention, the Court of Appeal referred, inter alia, to the presumption established under Article 258 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and held that that presumption alone justified the applicant's continued detention. It also held that keeping the applicant in custody was necessary in order to prevent him from interfering with the trial, given the reasonable risk of such interference which flowed from the fact that he had been charged with commission of offences as a member of an organised criminal group.

By [DATE_TIME] the trial court had held some 135 hearings of the 162 which had been scheduled. It heard more than 400 witnesses.

During the trial the applicant filed numerous but unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. He maintained that the length of his detention was excessive and that the charges against him lacked a sufficiently strong basis.

On [DATE_TIME] the Gdańsk Regional Court made a severance order with a view to expediting the proceedings, and thereafter four defendants (J.N., G.P., [LOCATION] and [PERSON]), who in the meantime had been released from detention, were to be tried separately.

After [DATE_TIME] no hearing was held due to the serious illness of the judge rapporteur. On [DATE_TIME] the President of the IV Criminal Section of the Gdańsk Regional Court assigned a new judge rapporteur. Consequently, the trial had to commence de novo.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until [DATE_TIME]. The applicant appealed against that decision. On [DATE_TIME] a different panel of the Court of Appeal quashed the impugned decision and ordered the applicant's release under police supervision. It also imposed on him a prohibition on leaving the country. The Court of Appeal had regard to the fact that the trial had to commence de novo and that the applicant had already spent [DATE_TIME] in pre-trial detention.

The applicant was released on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the trial court made a further severance order and divided the case into eleven separate cases.

It appears that the proceedings are still pending before the first-instance court.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 59526/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the unreasonable length of the applicant's detention and of his trial to the Government. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents and subsequently Mr [PERSON] of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION]. The Szczecin Regional Prosecutor laid charges of large-scale fraud against the applicant. The applicant was convicted and sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and a fine. He argued that his detention was excessive and amounted to serving a prison sentence. On an appeal lodged by the applicant, the Poznań Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. The subsequent proceedings were conducted against two defendants, including the applicant. The Regional Court joined the proceedings in question to the other set of proceedings. The number of defendants increased to three. The retrial was to begin on [DATED_TIME], but was adjourned since one of the defendants had to undergo a psychiatric examination. On [DATE_TIME] the Szczecin Regional Court dismissed an application for release on bail or subject to other guarantees or conditions. The applicant appealed, invoking, inter alia, Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. He also maintained that his detention was so excessive that it amounted in reality to serving a prison sentence. The Court of Appeal upheld the contested order and prolonged the applicant's detention pending trial until [DATING_TIME]. The court noted that he faced an exceptionally heavy sentence, which had already been shown by the severity of the penalty originally imposed at first instance. The court considered that neither bail, nor police supervision nor any other guarantee would secure the proper course of the trial. It considered that the trial had not progressed because of his conduct. The applicant appealed, maintaining that there was no legal basis for keeping him in custody. But the Court of Appeal rejected the appeal and extended the applicant's detention until [DATE_TIME] The applicant had earlier evaded justice and had criminal relations with certain witnesses involved in the case. This indicated that detention was the only preventive measure which would effectively secure the proper course of the trial, the court said. The court added that the applicant had misconstrued Article 263 §§ 3 and 4 of the [Date_TIME) Code. It said that only the Supreme Court could prolong it beyond the maximum statutory period laid down in paragraph 3 of that provision, but that rule applied only as long as there had been no conviction. The applicant requested that the three sets of criminal proceedings conducted against him before the courts in [LOCATION], including the proceedings at issue, be transferred to other courts. On [DATE_TIME] his request was refused. The applicant's appeal, based on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, was rejected by the Court of Appeal. The court ordered the applicant's release on condition that he put up bail of PLN 30,000. He was released as he had paid the bail. The case was settled in the Polish High Court of Justice (HCJ) in Warsaw. The judge found that the applicant had evaded justice at the initial stage of the proceedings. The applicant was convicted of large-scale fraud and breach of official secrecy. He was sentenced to a cumulative sentence of [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and a fine. The applicant appealed. The Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal. The application was later dismissed. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights. The trial of the applicant was adjourned until September 18. It is unclear if the applicant will be granted bail pending the outcome of the case. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on September 17. The court has yet to rule on the appeal's appeal. Click here to read the transcript of the application.

Mr. [PERSON] assumed the office of President of the Chamber in accordance with Rule 21 para. 5. Mr. [PERSON], who was subsequently prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case, was replaced by the first substitute judge, Mrs. [PERSON]. On [DATE_TIME], Mr. [PERSON], acting in pursuance of Rule 24 para. 4, granted himself exemption from sitting on the case. In accordance with Rule 21 paras. 3 (b) and 5, Mr. [PERSON], the Vice-President of the Court, became a full member of the Chamber and assumed the office of President of the Chamber.

The President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government and the Delegates of the Commission regarding the procedure to be followed. By an Order of 17 October, the President of the Chamber decided that the Government should file a memorial within a time-limit expiring on [DATE_TIME] and that the Delegates should be entitled to file a memorial in reply within [DATE_TIME] of receipt of the Government’s memorial.

The Government filed their memorial on [DATE_TIME]. The Secretary to the Commission advised the Deputy Registrar on [DATE_TIME] that the Delegates had decided not to file a memorial in reply; on [DATE_TIME], he communicated to the Registrar a note containing “the applicants’ observations on the question of the application of Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention“ and Mr. [PERSON]’s observations on the Government’s suggestion that his case be severed from the other two and be struck out of the Court’s list.

After consulting, through the Deputy Registrar, the Agent of the Government and the Delegates of the Commission, the President of the Chamber decided by an Order of 11 March that the oral hearings should open on [DATE_TIME].

The Chamber held a preparatory meeting on [DATE_TIME], immediately before the opening of the hearings. At that meeting the Chamber, granting a request presented by the Government, decided that their Agent and counsel could plead in [NRP] at the hearings, the Government undertaking, inter alia, responsibility for the interpretation into French or English of their oral arguments or statements (Rule 27 para. 2). At the same time, the Chamber took note of the intention of the Commission’s Delegates to be assisted during the oral proceedings by Mr. [PERSON], the lawyer of one of the applicants; it also authorised Mr. [PERSON] to speak in [NRP] (Rules 29 para. 1 in fine and 27 para. 3).

The oral hearings took place in public at [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. There appeared before the Court:

for the Government: Mrs. [PERSON], [PERSON] at the Federal Ministry of Justice, Agent, Mr. [PERSON], [PERSON] at the Federal Ministry of Justice, Mr. [PERSON], Richter am Landgericht, Federal Ministry of Justice, Advisers;

for the Commission: Mr. [PERSON], Principal Delegate, Mr. [PERSON], Delegate, Mr. [PERSON], lawyer for Mr. [PERSON], assisting the Delegates under Rule 29 para. 1, second sentence. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. [PERSON] for the Government and by Mr. [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON] for the Commission, as well as their replies to questions put by several judges.

On [DATE_TIME], the Agent of the Government supplemented in writing her reply to one of the questions that had been put to her. On [DATE_TIME], the Commission produced to the Court certain documents referred to by the Principal Delegate at the hearings; these documents were the subject of a letter, received on [DATE_TIME], from the Agent of the Government.

AS TO THE FACTS

At the time when they introduced their applications with the Commission, Mr. [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON] were resident in [LOCATION]. The three applicants were charged before the [NRP] courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with [NRP] law. After conviction, they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention.

I. THE DOMESTIC LAW

In criminal proceedings, the courts must use the services of an interpreter whenever the accused is not conversant with [NRP]. The first sentence of section 185 para. 1 of the Constitution of the Courts Act (Gerichtsverfassungsgesetz) provides as follows: “If the proceedings before the court involve the participation of persons who do not have command of the [NRP] language, an interpreter shall be employed.“ Pursuant to this provision, the assistance of an interpreter is made available as a matter of course to an accused - whatever his nationality - who does not understand or speak the [NRP] language. The same rule is applicable to the examination of witnesses who do not have command of the [NRP] language. The obligation to employ an interpreter is, however, subject to one exception, namely when all the participants are familiar with the foreign language (section 185 para. 2 of the Constitution of the Courts Act).

Interpretation costs are part of the costs of the proceedings which, according to Article 464 (a) para. 1, first sentence, of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Strafprozeßordnung), are made up of “the fees (Gebühren) and expenses of the Treasury“. The latter are listed in the Court Costs Act (Gerichtskostengesetz) which in turn refers to the Witnesses and Experts (Expenses) Act (Gesetz über die [PERSON] und Sachverständigen). Section 17 para. 2 of the last-mentioned Act provides that “for the purposes of compensation, interpreters shall be treated as experts“. According to Article 465 para. 1, first sentence, of the Code of Criminal Procedure: “The accused shall bear the costs of such part of the proceedings as concerned the act that gave rise to the conviction ...“ Under this provision, the question of payment of the costs of the proceedings arises only after there has been a final ruling on the guilt of the accused; an accused person may never be required to make any advance payment on these costs. In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. On the other hand, if the individual concerned is convicted, he has to pay the costs, but only such proportion thereof as relates to the criminal charges upheld by the court.

As concerns interpretation costs in particular, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention, which forms an integral part of the domestic law, specifies that “everyone charged with a criminal offence has the (right) ... to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court“. This text has not been interpreted and applied by the [NRP] courts in a uniform way. Certain courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear the costs in question for all time and in all cases; other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that while Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) - like the Code of Criminal Procedure - exempts an accused (that is, a person “charged with a criminal offence“) from paying in advance for the expenses incurred by the use of an interpreter, it does not prohibit such expenses being awarded against a convicted person.

Interpretation costs are assessed in accordance with a scale fixed by law and not by the interpreters themselves; the assessment is made by a court official ([PERSON]) when the overall costs of the proceedings are determined.

II. FACTS RELATING TO THE [LOCATION] APPLICANTS

1. Mr. [PERSON]

Mr. [PERSON] is a citizen of [LOCATION] and was, at the time of his application to the Commission, a member of the British Forces stationed in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME], the Bielefeld District Court (Amtsgericht) convicted him of a road traffic offence. He was fined DM 900 and ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings. On [DATE_TIME], after the judgment had become final, the public prosecutor’s department (Staatsanwaltschaft) attached to the Bielefeld Regional Court (Landgericht) served Mr. [PERSON] with a notice to pay the sum of DM 1,330.90, made up of the fine of DM 900 and the fees (Gebühren) due in respect of the criminal proceedings (DM 90) and the withdrawal of his driving licence (DM 30), together with police costs (DM 85.50) and interpretation costs (DM 225.40). DM 154.60 of the last item related to the oral hearing.

On [DATE_TIME], the applicant, represented by the Command Legal Aid Section at [LOCATION], entered an appeal ([PERSON]) against this assessment of costs; he maintained that the assessment was contrary to Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention in so far as it concerned payment of the interpretation costs. Following the refusal of the auditor (Bezirksrevisor) attached to the Bielefeld Regional Court to modify the assessment, the matter was referred to the Bielefeld District Court which dismissed the appeal on [DATE_TIME]. The District Court stated in particular: “The object of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention ... is to guarantee certain fundamental rights to everyone faced with criminal proceedings. In [LOCATION], this Article (art. 6) applies to proceedings brought against foreigners as well as to those brought against [NRP] nationals. It is not the aim of the provision to place foreigners in a more favourable position than [NRP] nationals. This, however, would be the case if a foreign convicted person was not required to pay the interpretation costs. For example, under the [NRP] law of procedure and costs, a deaf-and-dumb convicted person against whom proceedings cannot be taken without a special interpreter must pay the costs of interpretation. So must also a [NRP] convicted person in whose trial [NRP]-speaking witnesses have to be examined with the assistance of an interpreter. Under the rules of [NRP] criminal procedure every person finally convicted must himself bear all the costs of the proceedings, including ... the interpretation expenses. This obligation is not contrary to Article 6 (art. 6) ... which does not forbid awarding the costs of the proceedings against a person convicted of an offence. Under [NRP] procedural law, however, no accused person need make advance payment for the costs of interpreters ... This would appear not to be the case in other signatory [LOCATION] of the Convention as otherwise it would be difficult to understand the wording of Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e). The Court thus interprets Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) ... as a provisional exemption from paying the interpretation costs ...“

On [DATE_TIME], following an “immediate appeal“ (sofortige [PERSON]) by Mr. [PERSON], the Bielefeld Regional Court confirmed the impugned decision, relying, inter alia, on the “correctness of the reasoning“ contained in that decision. On [DATE_TIME], the applicant paid the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs.

2. Mr. [PERSON]

Mr. [PERSON] is an [NRP] citizen, born in [DATE_TIME]. After completing his apprenticeship as a locksmith in [LOCATION], he rejoined his father in [LOCATION] where he followed various occupations.

In [DATE_TIME], he was involved in a dispute in a [LOCATION] night-club during which another client lost his coat. He was charged with robbery and with assault occasioning bodily harm; his case was tried by the Berlin-Tiergarten Juvenile Court ([PERSON]). On [DATE_TIME], the Juvenile Court convicted him of assault occasioning bodily harm. He was sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment (Dauerarrest) - a sentence deemed to have been served during his detention on remand - and to a fine of DM 500, and he was ordered to pay the costs of the proceedings.

On [DATE_TIME], Mr. [PERSON] filed an “immediate appeal“ against the order as to costs insofar as the interpretation costs had been included in the award. He submitted that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention granted him exemption from payment of the costs in question. On [DATE_TIME], the Berlin Regional Court dismissed the appeal. The Regional Court reasoned that, since no assessment of costs had yet been made, there had been no decision capable of being challenged on appeal. The Regional Court further stated that the Juvenile Court would have acted improperly if it had omitted the interpretation costs from its decision on the costs of the proceedings - the former costs, according to Article 464 (a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure read in conjunction with the Court Costs Act and the Witnesses and Experts (Expenses) Act, constituting a component of the latter costs. Furthermore, it was added, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention did not prohibit a convicted person being made to bear interpretation costs.

On [DATE_TIME], [LOCATION] served Mr. [PERSON] with a notice to pay costs amounting to DM 665.63, including DM 321.95 for interpretation costs. The latter sum comprised the expenses incurred in respect of Mr. [PERSON]’s appearance before the judge on [DATE_TIME] (DM 33.25), the review on [DATE_TIME] of his detention on remand ([LOCATION]) (DM 67.60), the translation of the indictment (DM 90.20) and the trial hearing on [DATE_TIME] (DM 130.90). The applicant unsuccessfully challenged the inclusion of interpretation costs in this assessment of the costs. On [DATE_TIME], his appeal was dismissed by the District Court which held, inter alia, that Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention did not prevent interpretation costs being awarded against a convicted person. Mr. [PERSON] then lodged an “immediate appeal“ which was rejected by the Berlin Regional Court on [DATE_TIME]. As far as Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) was concerned, the Regional Court referred to its decision of [DATE_TIME] and continued: “In the light of the context of Article 6 para. 3 (art. 6-3) ..., which lays down fundamental guarantees for a fair trial, the Court ... interprets sub-paragraph (e) (art. 6-3-e) to mean that the assistance of an interpreter must not be made dependent on the accused’s making any advance payment. This sub-paragraph guarantees a court hearing for a foreigner who is ignorant of the language, regardless of his capacity to pay. Who finally has to bear the costs of interpretation after the proceedings have terminated is a different question. That after conviction this may be the accused is not excluded by Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) ...“

On [DATE_TIME], following a request by Mr. [PERSON], the Berlin Justizkasse allowed him to defer payment “until the decision of the Commission of Human Rights be known“. From that time, he has not been required to pay the costs in question since, at the request of the Government, the relevant [LOCATION] authorities (Landesjustizverwaltung) have suspended recovery awaiting the judgment of this Court.

3. Mr. [PERSON]

Mr. [PERSON], a [NRP] citizen born in [DATE_TIME], has been employed in [LOCATION] in various trades, including mining and the construction industry. When he applied to the Commission, he was living at [LOCATION]. On [DATE_TIME], he notified the relevant authorities in [LOCATION], near [LOCATION], his last place of residence in [LOCATION], of his intention to return to [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME], the Assize Court attached to the Regional Court ([NRP] beim Landgericht) at [LOCATION] convicted Mr. [PERSON] of causing grievous bodily harm. He was sentenced to a [DATE_TIME]’s imprisonment, but the balance of his sentence remaining after allowance had been made for his detention on remand was commuted to a period of probation. The court ordered the applicant to bear the costs of the proceedings “with the exception, however, of the costs occasioned by the assistance of the Turkish-language interpreter, which costs are to be borne by the Treasury“. Although taking notice of the conflicting practice of the [NRP] courts in this connection, the Assize Court held that the “free“ assistance of an interpreter, as guaranteed by Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) to every accused not conversant with the language of the court, is to be understood as being free once and for all time.

On an “immediate appeal“ by the public prosecutor’s department, the Cologne Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), in a fully reasoned decision delivered on [DATE_TIME], set aside the Assize Court’s judgment insofar as it related to the interpretation costs. The Court of Appeal stated: “On [its] wording, it is controversial whether (Article 6 para. 3 (e)) (art. 6-3-e) forbids a convicted person’s being charged with the costs of interpretation under the above-cited provisions relating to costs or whether - in the case of criminal proceedings in [NRP] courts – it merely means that the assistance of an interpreter may not be made dependent on an advance payment by the accused. ... ..... The object of the Convention is to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms against arbitrary State action and to place them under the protection of supranational law. ... It is not its purpose to go further and alter the national legal systems ... The list of procedural guarantees in Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention shows that the intention was to enshrine rights of the citizen and duties of the State which ensure a fair trial. This obviously means that the accused (or person charged) should be able to call for the assistance of an interpreter if he does not understand or speak the language used in court and that such assistance should be in no way dependent on the question of costs. But it certainly does not mean that even a convicted person may not have the costs of interpretation awarded against him. A fair trial is guaranteed in this respect insofar as the accused must be assisted by the interpreter he needs. The question whether he may later be required to bear the costs is not of the same order as the problem of guaranteeing human rights and fundamental freedoms but, both in theoretical and practical terms, is of lesser moment. It cannot be assumed that the Convention is intended to provide a piecemeal solution of the question of costs in criminal proceedings. Nor does the consideration that a foreigner should not receive worse treatment in the matter of costs than a national, dictate the conclusion that permanent exemption from costs is necessarily implied by the object of the Convention ... The Convention would not have come appreciably nearer to achieving its aim by prohibiting a financial disadvantage of such a kind.“ On [DATE_TIME], Mr. [PERSON] applied to the Federal Constitutional Court (Bundesverfassungsgericht) which, [DATE_TIME], declined to hear the application on the ground that it did not offer sufficient prospects of success.

According to the payment vouchers ([PERSON]), the fees paid to the interpreter amounted to DM 311.50 for the hearing on [DATE_TIME], DM 510.50 for the hearing on [DATE_TIME] and DM 112.50 for the hearing on [DATE_TIME] - making a total of DM 934.50.

Nevertheless, the applicant was not served with a notice to pay the costs for which he was liable, including the interpretation costs, since it was noted that he had a wife and four children to support, that his income was modest and that there was thus no prospect of recovering the costs. For these reasons, the competent court official, acting in pursuance of Article 10 para. 1 of the Service Instructions of 28 [DATE_TIME] on Court Costs (Kostenverfügung), had decided of his own motion on [DATE_TIME] not to assess the costs. His decision was not notified either to Mr. [PERSON] or to Mr. [PERSON]’s lawyer. A second decision to this effect was taken by the same official on [DATE_TIME]. This decision recorded that the applicant was living in [LOCATION] that his address was unknown and that recovery of the costs, being doomed to failure, should be waived. Mr. [PERSON]’s lawyer discovered the existence of the decision in [DATE_TIME] when he sought from the court a photocopy of the interpreter’s payment vouchers.

Before the Court, the Agent of the Government, with the agreement of the Minister of Justice for the Land of North-Rhine Westphalia made the following declaration: “... the compulsory collection of costs from the applicant Koç in pursuance of the judgment of [DATE_TIME] by the Assize Court attached to the Aachen Regional Court, varied in part by the decision of [DATE_TIME] by the Cologne Court of Appeal, will not be carried out in future; for the costs of such compulsory collection and the administrative costs would be out of proportion to the sum owed.“ The Agent specified that “the costs ... would not be collected even if the applicant were to return to [LOCATION]“. PROCEEDINGS BEFORE THE COMMISSION

In their applications, lodged respectively on [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME], Mr. [PERSON], Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON] claimed to be victims of a violation of Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention in that they had been ordered by the [NRP] courts to bear interpretation costs. Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON] also alleged discrimination by reason of the fact that a foreigner not speaking [NRP] was in a less favourable position than a [NRP] person.

The Commission declared Mr. [PERSON]’s application admissible on [DATE_TIME] and the applications of Mr. [PERSON] and Mr. [PERSON] admissible on [DATE_TIME] following. In its report of [DATE_TIME], the Commission expressed the opinion:

unanimously, that the decisions concerning the interpreter’s costs in the applicants’ cases were in breach of Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention;

by twelve votes to one, that it was not necessary to pursue its examination of the case under Article 14 (art. 14). The report contains one separate opinion. CONCLUDING SUBMISSIONS MADE TO THE COURT

In their memorial of [DATE_TIME], the Government

suggested that the Court, acting in pursuance of Rule 47 para. 2 of the Rules of Court, strike the case out of its list insofar as the applicant Koç was concerned;

requested the Court to find that [LOCATION] has not violated the Convention to the detriment of the applicants [PERSON] and [PERSON]. At the hearing on [DATE_TIME], the Government specified that this latter request applied also to Mr. [PERSON] if the Court did not comply with their above-mentioned suggestion.

name: Richard John Powell
train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on [DATE_TIME. The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 13 of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave, which was granted by the President of the Court, to be represented by a university law lecturer from [LOCATION] (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the convention) (art. 43) The hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [ LOCATION], on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr [PERSON] for the Government, by Mr. [Person) for the Commission and by Ms [P PERSON] forthe applicants, as well as their replies to its questions. There appeared before the Court: Mr  [PERSON], Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr  [PPerson], Counsel, [PIDENT], Department of Transport, Advisers; and Mr   ‘PERSON’, Lecturer in Law at the University of Essex, Counsel. Mr [PERSON]’s home fell just within the 35 Noise and Number Index (NNI) contour, which is considered to be a low noise-annoyance rating. Since [DATE_TIME] the house has been within a lower NNI contour. About 6,500 people around [LOCATION] experience a noise exposure equal to or greater than that suffered by Mr [Person] and his family. The NNI is a long-term average measure of noise exposure which is used to assess the disturbance from aircraft noise to communities near airports. It takes account of two features of the noise, namely the average noisiness and the number of aircraft heard. Land within the 35 to 39 NNI contours may be used for residential development, planning permission not being refused on noise grounds alone. No development whatsoever is permitted within the 60 NNI and over contours (high noise-annoyance zone) The Government’s policy, as stated in the [DATE_TIME] “Airports Policy“ White Paper, is that they are “not prepared to make any commitments at this stage on the question of a fifth terminal at [LOCATION] but will keep the matter under review“ (Command Paper, [PERSON], paragraph 5.19). The British Airports Authority, being a public statutory body, did not have power to acquire property near an airport. Intensification of an existing use is, for reasons of principle and practice, not compensatable. The liability of aircraft operators is further limited by section 76(1) of the Civil Aviation Act [DATE_TIME], which reads: “No action shall lie in respect of trespass or inrespect of nuisance, by reason only of the flight of an aircraft over any property at a height above the ground which, having regard to wind, weather and all the circumstances of the time, is causing annoyance through noise” Section 76(2) of the [DATE_TIME] Act in turn provides for strict liability - that is, liability without proof of intention or negligence - where material loss or damage to any person or property on land or water is caused by an aircraft in flight or an object falling from an aircraft. Section 76 is comparable to Article 1 of the Rome Convention of 1952 on Damage Caused by Foreign Aircraft to Third Parties on the Surface. The exemption applies only in respect of aircraft flying at a reasonable height above the ground. What is reasonable is a question of fact depending on all relevant circumstances. The Act does not exclude all liability on the part of aircraft operators for trespass and nuisance caused by planes in flight. The main forum for international co-operation seeking to make aircraft quieter is the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) The broad thrust of ICAO’s work has been towards the development of a series of standards, leading to the phasing out of aircraft unable to meet them. These standards are not operative within the I CAO member [LOCATION] unless and until they are given effect in national legislation. In the UK, effect is given to them by means of an Air Navigation (Noise Certification) Order. Heathrow Airport Limited has taken account of IFAO noise certification standards to encourage the use of quieter aircraft. Noise monitoring equipment is designed to protect the first built-up area reached after take-off from noise levels in excess of the statutory limits of 110 PNdB by day (07.00-23.00 hours local time) The Secretary of State is empowered by section 78 of the Civil Aviation Act to deny [LOCATION]’s facilities to operators who fail to comply with noise abatement measures, but to date it has not been found necessary to invoke this provision. The effect of recent bans on non-noise-certificated aircraft has been to keep the rate of compliance to around 99% by day and 98% by night. The application (no. 9310/81) was first lodged with the Commission on [DATE_TIME] by the Federation of Heathrow Anti-Noise Groups. Under this scheme, which cost the British Airports Authority approximately £19 million, over 16,000 house owners or occupiers applied for grants. In common with other persons living within the 60 NNI contour, Mr [PERSON] qualifies for a full noise-insulation grant. After consultation and in line with a commitment by the Government to review the boundaries once the actual noise climate was known, an extension scheme to include additional areas was brought into operation at an estimated cost of £11.25 million. At the public hearing on [DATE_TIME] the applicants asked the Court “to find that they have been the victims of a violation of Articles 6 and 8 (art. 6, art. 8) of the Convention’. They also submitted that “the applicants’ attempts to re-open their complaints under Articles 6. and 8 are ... entirely misconceived”. At the hearing the Government maintained the final conclusions in their memorial. The full text of the Commission’s opinion and of the dissenting opinion contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The decision was unanimous in favour of the applicants under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1.

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) on [DATE_TIME. The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 13 (art. 13) of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave, which was granted by the President of the Court, to be represented by a university law lecturer from [LOCATION] (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the convention) and Mr [Person), the President. The hearing took place in public in [LOCATION] on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by the Government, by the Commission and by the applicants. It also heard their replies to the Court's questions. The hearing was adjourned until the next day at [DATE_TIME] (Rule 38). The decision was returned and the case returned to the Registrar for further action. The case was heard by the Court of Appeal, which returned a decision in favour of the Government. The appeal was returned by the court of appeal and the decision was reversed on the basis of the decision of the Court, which was held to be unlawful. The applicant’s home fell just within the 35 Noise and Number Index (NNI) contour, which is considered to be a low noise-annoyance rating. Since [DATE_TIME] the house has been within a lower NNI contour. About half a million other people live within this contour area. About 6,500 people around [LOCATION] experience a noise exposure equal to or greater than that suffered by Mr [PERSON] and his family. The NNI is a long-term average measure of noise exposure which is used in [ LOCATION] to assess the disturbance from aircraft noise to communities near airports. Planning permission not being refused on noise grounds alone. Land within the 40 to 50 NNI contours (moderate noise-annoyance zone) will not be given over to development, except for infilling of existing built-up areas. No development whatsoever is permitted within the 60 NNI and over contours. Government’s policy, as stated in the [DATE_TIME] “Airports Policy“ White Paper, is that they are “not prepared to make any commitments at this stage on the question of a fifth terminal at [LOCATION] but will keep the matter under review“ Airport provides direct employment for some 48,600 persons, and pays over £16 million in local rates and rents. Intensification of an existing use is, for reasons of principle and practice, not compensatable. Mr and Mr [PERSON] would have no entitlement to compensation under this Act, there being no relevant new or altered development in the case of [LOCATION]. The liability of aircraft operators is further limited by section 76(1) of the Civil Aviation Act [DATE_TIME], which reads: “No action shall lie in respect of trespass or inrespect of nuisance, by reason only of the flight of an aircraft over any property at a height above the ground”. Section 76(2) of the [DATE_TIME] Act provides for strict liability without proof of intention or negligence. This is where material loss or damage to any person or property on land or water is caused by, inter alia, an aircraft in flight or an object falling from an aircraft. Section 76 is comparable to Article 1 of the Rome Convention of 1952 on Damage Caused by Foreign Aircraft to Third Parties on the Surface, which reads: “Any person who suffers damage on the surface shall, upon proof only, be entitled to compensation as provided by this Convention’” But there is no right to compensation if the damage is not a direct consequence of the incident giving rise to it. These standards are not operative within the I CAO member [LOCATION] unless and until they are given effect in national legislation. In the [ LOCATION] effect is given to them by means of an Air Navigation (Noise Certification) Order. A [DATE_TIME] Order gave effect to new ICAo standards and to regulations based upon recommendations of the European Civil Aviation Conference. Noise monitoring is designed to protect the first built-up area reached after take-off from noise levels in excess of the statutory limits of 110 PNdB by day (07.00-23.00 hours local time) The Secretary of State is empowered by section 78 of the Civil Aviation Act to deny [LOCATION]’s facilities to operators who fail to comply with noise abatement measures, but to date it has not been found necessary to invoke this provision. A scheme for sound insulation of dwellings was introduced for [LOCATION] in [DATE_TIME]. Under this scheme, which cost the British Airports Authority approximately £19 million, over 16,000 house owners or occupiers applied for grants. PROCEDURE

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) on [DATE_TIME], within the [DATE_TIME] period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 9310/81) against [LOCATION] [LOCATION] and [LOCATION] initially lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention on [DATE_TIME] by the Federation of Heathrow Anti-Noise Groups, which application was subsequently continued by [PERSON] and [PERSON], who are [NRP] citizens. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby [LOCATION] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 13 (art. 13) of the Convention.

The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr [PERSON], the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On [DATE_TIME], in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other five members, namely Mr [PERSON], Mr L.-E. [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). Subsequently, Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON], being unable to take part in the consideration of the case, were replaced by Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON], substitute judges; Mr [PERSON] was in turn replaced by Mr [PERSON] (Rules 22 § 1 and 24 § 1).

Mr [PERSON] assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 5) and, through the Deputy Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the representative of the applicants on the need for a written procedure (Rule 37 § 1). In accordance with the order made in consequence, the registry received the applicants’ memorial on [DATE_TIME] and the Government’s memorial on [DATE_TIME]. In a letter of [DATE_TIME], the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing.

Having consulted, through the Deputy Registrar, those who would be appearing before the Court, the President directed that the oral proceedings should open on [DATE_TIME] (Rule 38).

The hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on the appointed day. The Court had held a preparatory meeting immediately beforehand. There appeared before the Court:

for the Government Mr [PERSON], Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr [PERSON], [PERSON], Counsel, [PERSON], Department of Transport, Mr [PERSON], Department of Transport, Advisers;

Various documents were lodged at the registry by the Government and the applicants on [DATE_TIME] of the hearing and on different dates [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME].

AS TO THE FACTS

A. Background

The first applicant, [PERSON], is a director of a mining concern and lives with his family at Esher, [LOCATION], in a house which he bought in [DATE_TIME]. The property is situated several miles from [LOCATION], [LOCATION]. Since [DATE_TIME] it has lain under a flight departure route from [LOCATION] in operation for about one third of the year, usually during [DATE_TIME]. Following objections to the level of noise disturbance, the route was divided into two sections in [DATE_TIME]. At least until [DATE_TIME] Mr [PERSON]’s home fell just within the 35 Noise and Number Index (NNI) contour, which is considered to be a low noise-annoyance rating (see paragraph 10 below). About half a million other people live within this contour area. Since [DATE_TIME] the house has been within a lower NNI contour.

The second applicant, [PERSON], farms together with other members of his family lands situated in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], which have been in his family for some generations. He lives in a bungalow at [LOCATION] acquired by his family as part of its land-holding in [DATE_TIME]. The applicant took up residence there in [DATE_TIME] on the occasion of his marriage. The bungalow is situated about one and a third miles west of, and in a direct line with, [LOCATION]’s northern runway. It is regularly overflown during [DATE_TIME] and to a limited extent at [DATE_TIME]. It falls within a 60 NNI contour, which is regarded as an area of high noise-annoyance for residents. According to the statistics supplied by the Government, the average height of arriving aircraft over Mr [PERSON]’s property is 450 feet and the average height of departing aircraft varies between 1,235 and 2,365 feet according to aircraft type. About 6,500 people around [LOCATION] experience a noise exposure equal to or greater than that suffered by Mr [PERSON] and his family.

The NNI is a long-term average measure of noise exposure which is used in [LOCATION] to assess the disturbance from aircraft noise to communities near airports. It takes account of two features of the noise, namely the average noisiness and the number of aircraft heard during [DATE_TIME]. The flights which determine the NNI at any point on the ground are those which take place between 06.00 and 18.00 hours [LOCATION] Mean Time during the [DATE_TIME] to [DATE_TIME] and which make a peak noise level exceeding 80 perceived noise decibels (PNdB) at that point. The purpose of the NNI is to represent community reaction to the level of aircraft noise so as to guide planning, development and noise control. Thus, the NNI is amongst the criteria applied in planning controls, so that land within the 35 to 39 NNI contours may be used for residential development, planning permission not being refused on noise grounds alone. However, land within the 40 to 50 NNI contours (moderate noise-annoyance zone) will not be given over to development, except for the infilling of existing built-up areas on condition that appropriate sound insulation is used. No development whatsoever is permitted within the 60 NNI and over contours (high noise-annoyance zone). It is to be noted that the NNI calculation reflects a logarithmic element in the PNdB scale, which has the result that every increase of 10 in that scale represents approximately a doubling of the loudness.

B. The growth of [LOCATION]

[LOCATION] was formally opened in [DATE_TIME]. In [DATE_TIME] the first scheduled air services using jet airliners were inaugurated. Three terminals were opened in [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. After a public inquiry which lasted for [DATE_TIME] and heard 125 witnesses, a fourth terminal was opened in [DATE_TIME]. As regards future expansion, the Government’s policy, as stated in the [DATE_TIME] “Airports Policy“ White Paper, is that they are “not prepared to make any commitments at this stage on the question of a fifth terminal at [LOCATION] but will keep the matter under review“ (Command Paper, [PERSON], paragraph 5.19).

[LOCATION] is one of the busiest international airports in the world. The Airport handled 3 million passengers in [DATE_TIME], over one million passengers during [DATE_TIME], 22.4 million passengers on international routes and 4.4 million passengers on domestic routes in [DATE_TIME], and 37.5 million passengers on international routes and 6.8 million passengers on domestic routes in [DATE_TIME]. There has been a corresponding increase in aircraft movements over [DATE_TIME]. Over 22% of passengers use the airport as an interchange point. It is currently used by over 70 airlines and serves 200 destinations worldwide. It is [LOCATION] leading port in terms of visible trade and in [DATE_TIME] handled cargo valued at £26.3 billion. [LOCATION] contributes around £200 million to [LOCATION]’s balance of payments, provides direct employment for some 48,600 persons, in addition to the substantial number of workers employed locally in servicing the industry, and pays over £16 million in local rates and rents.

C. Compensation measures

Compensation for the loss of value of houses and land as a result of airport noise is provided for by the Land Compensation Act [DATE_TIME]. However, such compensation is payable only in respect of new or altered public works first brought into use after [DATE_TIME]. Intensification of an existing use is, for reasons of principle and practice, not compensatable. Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] would have no entitlement to compensation under this Act, there being no relevant new or altered development in the case of [LOCATION].

The British Airports Authority, being a public statutory body, did not have power to acquire property near an airport unless it could show that the acquisition of the property was necessary for the proper performance of its function. In [DATE_TIME], after the completion of the fourth terminal (see paragraph 11 above) and privatisation of the Authority, the successor company to the Authority announced a scheme for the purchase of noise-blighted properties close to [LOCATION]. This scheme provided for purchase by the company of property severely affected by aircraft noise at [LOCATION] (within the 65 NNI contour) where the owner had acquired the property before [DATE_TIME] and wished to sell but could not do so except at a deflated price. Claims had to be made [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. By virtue of the contour limitation the applicants’ properties were excluded from the scheme.

An action will lie at common law for nuisance in respect of an activity which unreasonably interferes with the use and enjoyment of land, for example an activity causing annoyance through noise. If liability is established, damages may be awarded or, in certain circumstances, an injunction granted. However, the Noise Abatement Act [DATE_TIME] specifically exempts aircraft noise from its protection. The liability of aircraft operators is further limited by section 76(1) of the Civil Aviation Act [DATE_TIME], which reads: “No action shall lie in respect of trespass or in respect of nuisance, by reason only of the flight of an aircraft over any property at a height above the ground which, having regard to wind, weather and all the circumstances of the case, is reasonable, or the ordinary incidents of such flights, so long as the provisions of any Air Navigation Order or of any orders under section 62 above have been duly complied with and there has been no breach of section 81 below.“ Section 76(2) of the [DATE_TIME] Act in turn provides for strict liability - that is, liability without proof of intention or negligence - where material loss or damage to any person or property on land or water is caused by, inter alia, an aircraft in flight or an object falling from an aircraft. Provisions equivalent to section 76 existed in earlier civil aviation legislation (for example, section 9 of the Air Navigation Act 1920 and section 40 of the Civil Aviation Act [DATE_TIME]). Section 76 is comparable to Article 1 of the Rome Convention of 1952 on Damage Caused by Foreign Aircraft to Third Parties on the Surface, which reads: “Any person who suffers damage on the surface shall, upon proof only that the damage was caused by an aircraft in flight or by any person or thing falling therefrom, be entitled to compensation as provided by this Convention. Nevertheless there shall be no right to compensation if the damage is not a direct consequence of the incident giving rise thereto, or if the damage results from the mere fact of passage of the aircraft through the airspace in conformity with existing air traffic regulations.“ (United Nations Treaty Series, [DATE_TIME], vol. 310, no. 4493, p. 182) As at [DATE_TIME], this Convention had been ratified by thirty-six States, including four members of the Council of Europe, namely [LOCATION], [LOCATION], [LOCATION] and [LOCATION] but not [LOCATION].

Section 76(1) of the [DATE_TIME] Act does not exclude all liability on the part of aircraft operators for trespass and nuisance caused by aircraft in flight. In the first place, the exemption applies only in respect of aircraft flying at a reasonable height above the ground. What is reasonable is a question of fact depending on all relevant circumstances. Secondly, for the exemption to apply there must be compliance with the statutory provisions referred to in section 76(1). In practice this means the Air Navigation Order [DATE_TIME] as amended, the Air Navigation (General) Regulations 1981 as amended, the Rules of the Air and Air Traffic Control Regulations [DATE_TIME] as amended and, of especial importance in this connection, the Air Navigation (Noise Certification) Order [DATE_TIME] (and the corresponding provisions of earlier orders and regulations applicable from time to time). Thus, if, for example, an aircraft flies in a manner which is not in accordance with the applicable regulations or takes off or lands in contravention of the Air Navigation (Noise Certification) Order, its operator will not be entitled to rely upon section 76 as a defence to any action for trespass or nuisance.

The main forum for international co-operation seeking to make aircraft quieter is the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO). The broad thrust of ICAO’s work has been towards the development of a series of standards, leading to the phasing out of aircraft unable to meet them. These standards are not operative within the ICAO member [LOCATION] unless and until they are given effect in national legislation. In the [LOCATION] effect is given to them by means of an Air Navigation (Noise Certification) Order. Orders of [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] reflected the first ICAO standards developed concerning subsonic jet aircraft. A [DATE_TIME] Order gave effect to new ICAO standards and to regulations based upon recommendations of the European Civil Aviation Conference. Orders of [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] introduced further ICAO standards.

Since [DATE_TIME] restrictions have been placed on [DATE_TIME] movements of jets, with the aim of phasing out night flights of noisier aircraft. These measures have been adopted in the light of research into the relationship between aircraft noise and sleep disturbance and after consultation of all interested parties, including the Federation of Heathrow Anti-Noise Groups to which the applicants belong.

Monitoring of aircraft noise on take-off from [LOCATION] was first carried out in [DATE_TIME]. Since [DATE_TIME] automatic equipment, consisting of thirteen noise monitoring terminals linked to a central processing and control unit, has been used. The positioning of these terminals is designed to protect the first built-up area reached after take-off from noise levels in excess of the statutory limits of 110 PNdB by day (07.00-23.00 hours local time) and 102 PNdB by [DATE_TIME] ([DATE_TIME] local time). Furthermore, minimum height requirements on approach to land as well as on take-off are laid down in the regulations. In addition, since [DATE_TIME] a system of regularly alternating the landing runway has been implemented at [LOCATION] during westerly operations, the main objective being to achieve a fair sharing of periods of relative quiet among the communities of [LOCATION] affected by noise from landing aircraft.

Owing to his strong propensity to commit crimes, there was a risk that he might commit further violent sexual offences, in particular rapes. The judge quashed the decision of the Regional Court and decided to retransfer the applicant to prison in accordance with Article 67a § 3 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 37 below) The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal as ill‑founded. He complained, in particular, that the psychiatric expert report on which the decisions had been based had not complied with the minimum standards to be met by such reports. The conditions of his detention during the execution of the preventive detention were also unsatisfactory. The man was sentenced to two years in prison for an alleged sexual assault. Transfer for enforcement of a different measure of correction and prevention. The case-law was subsequently reversed (see paragraphs 41-45 below).
