I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES

The details concerning the date of birth and place of residence of the five applicants are contained in their application forms and are available in the respective case files.

Each applicant failed to pay sums due in respect of either local taxes (community charge or council tax), or court-imposed fines. In respect of the failure to pay local taxes, the magistrates’ court had in each case determined that the applicant was liable to pay (issuing a “liability order”); in fines cases, the magistrates’ court had imposed the fine as the sentence following a criminal conviction.

Each applicant fell into arrears with the payments due from them. These cases involve the enforcement proceedings in respect of their arrears in the magistrates’ court. Each applicant appeared before the court, following the issuing of an application for their committal to prison as a result of their failure to pay the sums due. At that hearing the magistrates found that the non-payment was due to the applicant’s wilful refusal or culpable neglect. As a result each applicant was sentenced to a period of imprisonment, suspended on terms that the applicant make periodic payments towards the outstanding sum. The applicants failed to comply with the terms imposed. A further hearing was thereafter held in the magistrates’ court at which the suspended term of imprisonment was activated. Each applicant spent a period of time in prison. Legal aid (free legal representation where the applicant did not have sufficient means to pay for it) was not available for these enforcement proceedings prior to 1 [DATE_TIME] and none of the applicants was legally represented at the hearings in front of the magistrates.

Following their imprisonment, an application was made on behalf of each applicant, by way of either judicial review or case stated, which resulted in the High Court quashing the orders made by the magistrates. The applicants were released from prison on bail at the time of making their applications to the High Court. In all five cases the orders were quashed following the High Court’s approval of a consent order agreed between the applicants and the magistrates who had sentenced them.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on [DATE_TIME. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention (art. 6-1). The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the convention) and Mr [Person), the President of the Court. The applicant, [PERSON], is a [NRP] citizen who was born in [DATE_TIME] and now lives in [LOCATION] [ LOCATION]. He joined the army and became a member of the Scots Guards. As a result of these experiences he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder (“PTSD”) This disorder was not diagnosed until after the events of [Date_TIME) (Rule 37 para. 1). The hearing took place in public in [ Location], [LOCation], on [D date_TIME]. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government [Person], Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr [P PERSON] QC. The applicant, who had become a lance-sergeant, was sent with his regiment to [LOCATION]. On [DATE_TIME], after a heavy drinking session, he held members of his own unit at pistol point and threatened to kill himself and some of his colleagues. He fired two shots, which were not aimed at anyone and hit a television set, and subsequently surrendered the pistol. He was then arrested and charged with a number of offences. The applicant was found to be fit to plead and knew what he was doing at the time of the incident. However, his chronic back problem (which caused him to be frustrated and depressed at not being fit for duty) together with “his previous combat stresses and a very high level of alcohol ... combined to produce this dangerous behaviour“. Mr [PERSON] was also examined by Dr [Person], at the request of his solicitor. She confirmed that the consumption of alcohol on [DATE_TIME] was a result of his condition and not a cause of it. He was remanded for trial on eight charges and decided that he should be tried by general court martial. The composition of the court martial consisted of a president and four other members: (1) the president was a member of London District staff (under the command of the convening officer: see paragraph 14 above) and was not a permanent president. (2) a Lieutenant-Colonel was a permanent member of courts martial, sitting in the capacity of an ordinary member. (3) a Captain was from the Coldstream Guards, a unit stationed in [LOCATION]. He was appointed by his commanding officer. The judge advocate for the general court martial was appointed by the Judge Advocate General (see paragraphs 42-45 below) The defence put before the court the medical reports referred to above (paragraphs 11-13) and called Dr [PERSON] to give evidence. Mr [Person] pleaded guilty to three charges of common assault (a civilian offence), two charges of conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline (a military offence) and two counts of threatening to kill. The court martial hearing was adjourned by the judge advocate general after the defence argued that he was not responsible for his actions and that he had been counselled. The prosecution did not call any medical evidence in rebuttal or adopt any of the evidence prepared by the army-instructed psychiatrists. Mr [PERSON]’s solicitor urged the court martial that, in view of the fact that his client had been suffering from PTSD at the time of the incident and was extremely unlikely to reoffend, he should be allowed to complete his service. The court martial sentenced the applicant to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment, reduction to the rank of guardsman and dismissal from the army (which caused him to suffer a reduction in his pension entitlement). No reasons were given for the sentence (see paragraph 46 below). The judge advocate's advice was not disclosed to the applicant, nor was he given reasons for the decisions confirming his sentence and rejecting his petitions. The civil action was settled by the Secretary of State for Defence, who paid the applicant £100,000 and legal costs, without any admission of liability. Mr [PERSON] commenced a civil claim in negligence against the military authorities, claiming damages in respect of his back injury and PTSD. In a report dated [DATE_TIME] prepared for these purposes, Dr [Person] confirmed her previous opinion (see paragraph 12 above) and clearly diagnosed PTSD. The settlement did not differentiate between the claims inrespect of PTSD and the back injury.

The President drew by lot the names of the other seven members of the Chamber (Art. 43 in fine) The applicant, [PERSON], is a [NRP] citizen who was born in [DATE_TIME] in [LOCATION], [ LOCATION] and now lives in [ LOCation] [LOCation]. He joined the army and became a member of the Scots Guards. He was injured in the wrist by a mortar-shell blast. As a result of these experiences he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder (‘PTSD’) which manifested itself by flashbacks, nightmares, feelings of anxiety, insomnia and outbursts of anger. This disorder was not diagnosed until after the events of [DATING_TIME]. His service was due to terminate in either [Dating_TIME], when he would have received a resettlement grant and an army pension. The applicant, who had become a lance-sergeant, was sent with his regiment to [LOCATION]. He was remanded for trial on eight charges arising out of the incident of [DATE_TIME] and decided that he should be tried by general court martial. PROCEDURE

The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) on [DATE_TIME], within the three‑month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention (art. 32-1, art. 47). It originated in an application (no. 22107/93) against [LOCATION] [LOCATION] and [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr [PERSON], a [NRP] citizen, on [DATE_TIME]. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and [DATE_TIME] (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby [LOCATION] recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention (art. 6-1).

In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30).

The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir [PERSON], the elected judge of [NRP] nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr [PERSON], the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 4 (b)). On [DATE_TIME], in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr [PERSON], Mrs [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 5) (art. 43).

As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6), Mr [PERSON], acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the United Kingdom Government (“the Government“), the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and [DATE_TIME]). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial on [DATE_TIME] and the Government’s memorial on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the President decided to admit to the Court file an additional memorial submitted by the applicant which had been received by the Registrar on [DATE_TIME] (Rule 37 para. 1).

In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], on [DATE_TIME]. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government [PERSON], Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr [PERSON] QC, Mr [PERSON], Barrister-at-Law, Counsel, Mr [PERSON], Ministry of Defence, Ms [PERSON], Ministry of Defence, Mr [PERSON], Ministry of Defence, Advisers; (b) for the Commission Mr [PERSON], Delegate, (c) for the applicant Mr [PERSON], Solicitor, Counsel, Mr [PERSON], Solicitor, Mr [PERSON], Solicitor, Advisers. The Court heard addresses by Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON].

AS TO THE FACTS

I. Circumstances of the case

The applicant, [PERSON], is a [NRP] citizen who was born in [DATE_TIME] in [LOCATION], [LOCATION], and now lives in [LOCATION] [LOCATION].

In [DATE_TIME] he joined the [NRP] army and became a member of the Scots Guards. His service was due to terminate in [DATE_TIME] or [DATE_TIME] when he would have received a resettlement grant and, at [DATE_TIME], an army pension.

In [DATE_TIME] Mr [PERSON] took part in the [LOCATION] campaign. During the battle of [LOCATION] he witnessed the death and mutilation of several of his friends and was himself injured in the wrist by a mortar-shell blast. According to the medical evidence prepared for his court martial (see paragraphs 11-13 below), as a result of these experiences he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder (“PTSD“), which manifested itself by flashbacks, nightmares, feelings of anxiety, insomnia and outbursts of anger. This disorder was not diagnosed until after the events of [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 10 below).

In [DATE_TIME] he sustained an injury during training for service in [LOCATION] when a rope which he was climbing broke and he fell to the ground, severely damaging his back. This injury was extremely painful and affected his ability to perform his duties, which, again according to the medical evidence, led him to suffer from feelings of stress, guilt and depression.

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant, who had become a lance-sergeant, was sent with his regiment to [LOCATION]. On [DATE_TIME], after a heavy drinking session, he held members of his own unit at pistol point and threatened to kill himself and some of his colleagues. He fired two shots, which were not aimed at anyone and hit a television set, and subsequently surrendered the pistol. He was then arrested.

1. The medical evidence

On [DATE_TIME] an ex-naval psychiatrist, Dr [PERSON], examined Mr [PERSON] and found that he was responsible for his actions at the time of the incident. However, a combination of stresses (including his back injury and posting to [LOCATION]) together with his heavy drinking on [DATE_TIME], had led to an “almost inevitable“ event. Dr [PERSON] recommended “awarding the minimum appropriate punishment“. Following this report, the decision was taken to charge Mr [PERSON] with a number of offences arising out of the incident on [DATE_TIME] (see paragraph 14 below).

In order to establish that he was fit to stand trial, at the request of the army he was examined on two occasions by Dr [PERSON], a civilian consultant psychiatrist who had been employed by the Ministry of Defence since [DATE_TIME]. In her report of [DATE_TIME], Dr [PERSON] confirmed that Mr [PERSON] was fit to plead and knew what he was doing at the time of the incident. However, his chronic back problem (which caused him to be frustrated and depressed at not being fit for duty in his [LOCATION] posting) together with “his previous combat stresses and a very high level of alcohol ... combined to produce this dangerous behaviour“. In her second report, of [DATE_TIME], she explained that the applicant had reacted to the stress caused by his back problems in the way he did on [DATE_TIME] because of his experiences in the Falklands war. Whilst she did not clearly state that he suffered from PTSD, she confirmed that similar patterns of behaviour frequently occurred at a late stage in those who experienced this disorder. She confirmed that the consumption of alcohol on [DATE_TIME] was a result of his condition and not a cause of it.

Mr [PERSON] was also examined by Dr [PERSON], at the request of his (Mr [PERSON]’s) solicitor. Dr [PERSON] diagnosed him as suffering from PTSD as a result of his service in the [LOCATION].

2. The composition of the court martial

The position of “convening officer“ (see paragraphs 36-41 below) for the applicant’s court martial was assumed by the General Officer Commanding [LOCATION], Major General [PERSON]. He remanded Mr [PERSON] for trial on eight charges arising out of the incident of [DATE_TIME] and decided that he should be tried by general court martial.

By an order dated [DATE_TIME], the convening officer convened the general court martial and appointed the military personnel who were to act as prosecuting officer, assistant prosecuting officer and assistant defending officer (to represent Mr [PERSON] in addition to his solicitor) and the members of the court martial (see paragraph 37 below).

The court martial consisted of a president and four other members: (1) the president, Colonel [PERSON], was a member of London District staff (under the command of the convening officer: see paragraph 14 above). He was appointed by name by the latter and was not a permanent president; (2) Lieutenant-Colonel [PERSON] was a permanent president of courts martial, sitting in the capacity of an ordinary member. He had his office in the London District Headquarters. He was appointed by name by the convening officer; (3) Captain [PERSON] was from the Coldstream Guards, a unit stationed in [LOCATION]. His reporting chain was to his officer commanding, his commanding officer and the Brigade Commander, after which his report could, in exceptional circumstances, go to the convening officer; he was a member of a footguard unit and the convening officer, as General Officer Commanding, was responsible for all footguard units. He was appointed to the court martial by his commanding officer; (4) Major [PERSON] was from the Grenadier Guards, also a footguard unit stationed in [LOCATION]. The convening officer was his second superior reporting officer. He was appointed to the court martial by his commanding officer; (5) Captain [PERSON] was from the Postal and Courier Department, Royal Engineers (Women’s Royal Army Corps), which is under the direct command of the Ministry of Defence and is administered by [LOCATION]. She was appointed by her commanding officer. In summary, all of the members of the court martial were subordinate in rank to the convening officer and served in units stationed within [LOCATION]. None of them had legal training.

The assistant prosecuting and defending officers were both officers from the Second Scots Guards stationed in [LOCATION] and had the same reporting chain as Captain [PERSON] (see paragraph 16 (3) above).

The judge advocate for the general court martial was appointed by the Judge Advocate General (see paragraphs 42-45 below). He was a barrister and assistant judge advocate with the Judge Advocate General’s Office.

3. The court martial hearing

On [DATE_TIME], Mr [PERSON] appeared before the general court martial, at [LOCATION] in [LOCATION]. He was represented by a solicitor. He pleaded guilty to three charges of common assault (a civilian offence), two charges of conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline (a military offence) and two charges of threatening to kill (a civilian offence).

On [DATE_TIME], his solicitor had made a written request to the prosecuting authorities to ensure the appearance of Dr [PERSON] at the court martial and on [DATE_TIME] the prosecuting officer had issued a witness summons requiring her attendance. However, the defence was informed on [DATE_TIME] of the hearing that Dr [PERSON] would not be attending. Mr [PERSON] claims that her absence persuaded him to plead guilty to the above charges. However, his solicitor did not request an adjournment or object to the hearing proceeding.

The defence put before the court martial the medical reports referred to above (paragraphs 11-13) and called Dr [PERSON] to give evidence. The latter confirmed his view that the applicant suffered from PTSD, that this had been the principal cause of his behaviour, that he had not been responsible for his actions and that he was in need of counselling. During cross‑examination, Dr [PERSON] stated that this was the first time he had dealt with battle-related PTSD. The prosecution did not call any medical evidence in rebuttal or adopt any of the evidence prepared by the army-instructed psychiatrists, [PERSON] and [PERSON] (see paragraphs 11-13 above).

In the course of his speech in mitigation, Mr [PERSON]’s solicitor urged the court martial that, in view of the fact that his client had been suffering from PTSD at the time of the incident and was extremely unlikely to reoffend, he should be allowed to complete [DATE_TIME] of his service and leave the army with his pension intact and a minimal endorsement on his record.

Having heard the evidence and speeches, the court martial retired to consider their decision on sentence, accompanied by the judge advocate. On their return they sentenced the applicant to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment, reduction to the rank of guardsman and dismissal from the army (which caused him to suffer a reduction in his pension entitlement). No reasons were given for the sentence (see paragraph 46 below).

4. The confirmation of sentence and review process

Under the Army Act [DATE_TIME], the decision of the court martial had no effect until it was confirmed by the “confirming officer“ (see paragraph 48 below). In Mr [PERSON]’s case, as was usual practice, the confirming officer was the same person as the convening officer. Mr [PERSON] petitioned him for a reduction in sentence. Having received advice from the Judge Advocate General’s Office, the confirming officer informed the applicant on [DATE_TIME] that the sentence had been upheld.

The applicant, who had been under close arrest since [DATE_TIME] before the court martial hearing, was removed on [DATE_TIME] to a military prison and thereafter to a civilian prison on [DATE_TIME].

He appealed by way of petition to the first of the “reviewing authorities“ (see paragraph 49 below), the Deputy Director General of Personal Services, as delegate of the Army Board, a non-legally qualified officer who obtained advice from the Judge Advocate General’s Office. By a letter dated [DATE_TIME], Mr [PERSON] was informed that this petition had been rejected.

He then petitioned the second of the reviewing authorities, a member of the Defence Council who also was not legally qualified and who also received advice from the Judge Advocate General’s Office. This petition was rejected on [DATE_TIME].

The advice given by the Judge Advocate General’s Office at each of these three stages of review was not disclosed to the applicant, nor was he given reasons for the decisions confirming his sentence and rejecting his petitions.

On [DATE_TIME], the applicant applied to the Divisional Court for leave to challenge by judicial review the validity of the findings of the court martial. He claimed that the sentence imposed was excessive, the proceedings were contrary to the rules of natural justice and that the judge advocate had been hostile to him on two occasions during the hearing. On [DATE_TIME] the Divisional Court refused leave on the basis that the court martial had been conducted fully in accordance with the Army Act [DATE_TIME] and there was no evidence of improper conduct or hostility on the part of the judge advocate (R. v. General Court Martial (Regent’s Park Barracks), ex parte [PERSON], CO/1092/92, unreported).

5. Civil proceedings

Mr [PERSON] commenced a civil claim in negligence against the military authorities, claiming damages in respect of his back injury and PTSD. In a report dated [DATE_TIME] prepared for these purposes, Dr [PERSON] confirmed her previous opinion (see paragraph 12 above) and clearly diagnosed PTSD.

In [DATE_TIME] the civil action was settled by the Secretary of State for Defence, who paid the applicant £100,000 and legal costs, without any admission of liability. The settlement did not differentiate between the claims in respect of PTSD and the back injury.

The receiver sought to sell the applicant’s horses immediately and this was successfully challenged by the applicant. The Court of Appeal confirmed that the purpose of the [DATE_TIME] Act was to preserve the value of assets in the event of a conviction. The [DATE_TIME] Act provides for the making of a confiscation order in the event of a conviction for drug trafficking offences. The prosecution served notice under section 2 of the Act of its intention to seek a confiscations order. The defence failed to serve a written response to the prosecution’s statement within the period. The judge was informed that the delay in serving the defence response had been caused by the applicant moving prisons and wishing to instruct new solicitors. Prosecution counsel indicated that an extension of the deadline might be required. Defence counsel confirmed that the applicant wished to apply for a transfer to new soliciters and agreed an extension would probably be required as it was unlikely a fresh legal team would be ready by the current deadline. The judge granted a short adjournment of [DATE_TIME] to resolve the matter of transferring representation. The defence gave notice that it wished to challenge the validity of the postponement of the confiscation hearing. The judge set a timetable for the service of skeleton arguments on the jurisdiction point. A review hearing in the applicant’s case was scheduled for [DAT_TIME]. In the event, the pending appeal case was subsequently conceded by the prosecution so no oral argument took place in that case. The hearing was vacated as a result of informal discussions between junior counsel for both sides regarding a case pending before the Court of Appeal. Two defence applications were heard by newly instructed leading counsel. The first was to stay the confiscation proceedings on grounds of abuse of process. The second was for an order declaring that there was no jurisdiction to continue the proceedings. The judge indicated his preference for retention of [DATE_TIME] for the substantive hearing with any legal argument to take place beforehand. He indicated that alternative leading counsel could be found. in agreeing to vacate [Date_TIME]. counsel for the defence had understood that if the appeal in the other case was decided in the appellant’s favour, the prosecution in the applicant’'s case would terminate the confiscate proceedings against him. Judge ruled that no prejudice had been caused to the applicant as a result of the postponement. Accordingly, he concluded that the court had jurisdiction to deal with the confiscation proceedings. An appeal against that judgment was lodged with the House of Lords. For unknown reasons, matters proceeded more slowly than the parties had expected and the [DATE_TIME] confiscation hearing did not go ahead. A further judgment in a similar appeal was handed down by the Court of Appeal on [Date_TIME) (R v Knights ([PERSON]) and others]. EWCA Crim 2954). The parties were requested to keep the court updated. The applicant was subsequently informed by letter from the Court. of Appeal that a question had been certified for the House. of Lords in the case of Knights and others. Hearing held until House of Lords had not issued a judgment in Knights and others. Hearings were again postponed in [DATE_TIME] due to disclosure issues in relation to the receiver. Court was told that applicant had lodged an out-of-time appeal with the Court of Appeal against his conviction. There was little point in fixing a date for a substantive hearing in the confiscation proceedings. The judge agreed to the postponement on condition that the parties kept him informed of any progress in the meantime. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION]. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, can be summarised as follows.

A. The applicant’s arrest and trial

The applicant was arrested in the [LOCATION] on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME], following transfer to [LOCATION], he was charged with the attempted importation of 163 kilograms (compressed weight) of cocaine with a potential street value of GBP 11 million.

Prior to trial, in order to seize and preserve the applicant’s assets for future confiscation in the event of a conviction, the prosecution applied for and obtained a restraint order and the appointment of a receiver under section 26 of the Drug Trafficking Act [DATE_TIME] (“the [DATE_TIME] Act”). The receiver sought to sell the applicant’s horses immediately and this was successfully challenged by the applicant. In its judgment dated [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal confirmed that the purpose of the [DATE_TIME] Act was to preserve the value of assets for the purpose of future confiscation proceedings.

Also prior to trial, the applicant sought to challenge the admissibility of telephone interception evidence obtained in the [LOCATION]. He ultimately pursued an appeal to the House of Lords, which delivered its judgment against the applicant on [DATE_TIME].

The trial subsequently commenced in the Crown Court in [DATE_TIME]. However, after the jury had already retired to consider their verdict a prejudicial document was discovered within the jury bundle. The fault for this lay with the prosecution, a matter admitted at the time. Consequently, on [DATE_TIME] the jury were discharged.

A retrial commenced on [DATE_TIME]. At the start of the retrial the applicant’s counsel pursued an unsuccessful application to stay the proceedings on grounds of hardship suffered as a result of the prosecution’s negligence in causing the first trial to be abandoned.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was found guilty of the offences charged. On [DATE_TIME] he was sentenced to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment. He lodged an appeal against sentence, which was unsuccessful. In [DATE_TIME] he lodged an out-of-time appeal against conviction. He was released from prison in [DATE_TIME] and, on [DATE_TIME], he abandoned his appeal (see further paragraph 29 below).

The [DATE_TIME] Act provides for the making of a confiscation order in the event of a conviction for drug trafficking offences. Accordingly, prior to the sentencing hearing, the prosecution served notice under section 2 of the Act of its intention to seek a confiscation order and a statement under section 11 of the Act containing the prosecution’s assessment of whether the applicant had benefited from drug trafficking and the value of his proceeds of drug trafficking.

At this hearing, the judge was informed that the delay in serving the defence response had been caused by the applicant moving prisons and wishing to instruct new solicitors. The prosecution drew the judge’s attention to section 3 of the 1994 Act, which provided a [DATE_TIME] deadline in respect of the confiscation proceedings. The judge granted a short adjournment of [DATE_TIME] to resolve the matter of transferring representation.

The judge suggested a provisional date of [DATE_TIME] for the substantive confiscation hearing.

The judge set a timetable for the service of skeleton arguments on the jurisdiction point and fixed [DATE_TIME] for legal argument on the matter.

The judge reluctantly put back the substantive confiscation proceedings until [DATE_TIME], noting that he was “very loath to have further slippage than is absolutely necessary”.

The first was to stay the confiscation proceedings on grounds of abuse of process; the second was for an order declaring that there was no jurisdiction to continue the confiscation proceedings on account of the judge having failed to observe the proper procedural requirements when he postponed the confiscation hearing on [DATE_TIME].

In his ruling of [DATE_TIME] the judge found, in relation to the jurisdiction point that the original adjournment was to afford the defence more time, that no defence response had been forthcoming to the prosecution statement and that further delay had been caused by the applicant wishing to instruct new solicitors. He indicated that he had listed the case on [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] before the [DATE_TIME] time-limit expired, and that on that date he had postponed the listing to [DATE_TIME] in compliance with section 3 of the 1994 Act. He further found that no prejudice had been caused to the applicant as a result of the postponement. Accordingly, he concluded that the court had jurisdiction to deal with the confiscation proceedings. On the issue of abuse of process, the judge ruled that there had been a misunderstanding between counsel as to whether any undertaking had been given and that no abuse therefore arose. Following the ruling, the confiscation proceedings were adjourned and fixed for [DATE_TIME] to allow the defence to prepare their case.

Further argument then took place in relation to the jurisdiction point following a Court of Appeal judgment on [DATE_TIME] in which a confiscation order was quashed following a finding that a Crown Court judge had not complied with the requirements of section 3 of the 1994 Act. The applicant asked the judge to reconsider his ruling of [DATE_TIME]. The judge considered the applicant’s case to be distinguishable on the facts. However, on the request of the defence and following advice from both parties that an interlocutory appeal could be completed quickly and that the [DATE_TIME] confiscation hearing would not need to be vacated, he certified the point as fit for appeal to the Court of Appeal.

The applicant duly lodged an appeal on the jurisdiction point. For unknown reasons, matters proceeded more slowly than the parties had expected and the [DATE_TIME] confiscation hearing did not go ahead. A further judgment in a similar appeal was handed down by the Court of Appeal on [DATE_TIME] (R v Knights ([PERSON]) and others [[DATE_TIME]] EWCA Crim 2954). An appeal against that judgment was lodged with the House of Lords.

The applicant’s case was adjourned further in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] on application by him under section 3 of the 1994 Act, the “exceptional circumstances” being the pending House of Lords appeals. The parties were requested to keep the court updated. The applicant was subsequently informed by letter from the Court of Appeal dated [DATE_TIME] that a question had been certified for the House of Lords in the case of Knights and others and that all similar appeals, including his own, would be held in abeyance until that appeal had been decided by the House of Lords.

As a result of this, and disclosure issues in relation to the receiver, the matter was further postponed in [DATE_TIME] until [DATE_TIME] by which time the House of Lords had not issued a judgment in Knights and others. The judge allowed a [DATE_TIME] adjournment to obtain an update from the judicial office of the House of Lords. He was reminded by the applicant that he would again need to formally postpone the confiscation hearing. The judge proposed a further [DATE_TIME] postponement, on the proviso that he be provided with more up to date information in a [DATE_TIME]’s time and that if the proceedings could be listed and dealt with before the [DATE_TIME] period had expired, the parties should arrange this. Both counsel agreed.

Further hearings took place in [DATE_TIME]. However, the House of Lords had still not issued a judgment. Further postponements were ordered.

On [DATE_TIME] the judge was informed that the applicant had lodged an out-of-time appeal with the Court of Appeal against his conviction. Accordingly, there was little point in fixing a date for a substantive hearing in the confiscation proceedings. The applicant suggested a postponement to [DATE_TIME]. The judge agreed to the postponement on condition that the parties kept him informed of any progress in the meantime.

On [DATE_TIME] the House of Lords handed down their judgments in two jurisdiction appeals (R v Knights and others [[DATE_TIME]] UKHL 50; and R v [PERSON] and another [[DATE_TIME]] UKHL 49). It upheld the confiscation orders, stating that any prejudice caused to the defendants by delay was outweighed by the public interest in not allowing convicted offenders to escape confiscation for bona fide errors in the judicial process.

On [DATE_TIME] a procedural hearing was held in the Crown Court in the applicant’s case. The applicant’s counsel acknowledged that the House of Lords judgment effectively ruled out the prospect of a successful appeal on jurisdiction. The applicant requested a further adjournment to allow the parties to discuss matters further and agree amongst themselves a convenient date in [DATE_TIME] for the next hearing. The judge agreed to an adjournment. It is unclear whether a hearing took place in [DATE_TIME] or whether further adjournments were agreed in light of the applicant’s pending appeal against conviction.

In the meantime, from [DATE_TIME], separate hearings were held in the Court of Appeal relating to the applicant’s appeal against conviction. On [DATE_TIME], the applicant was released from prison, having served half of his sentence. On [DATE_TIME], apparently following adverse outcomes on various issues relating to his appeal, the applicant abandoned his appeal against conviction.

On [DATE_TIME] at a review hearing in the confiscation proceedings, the applicant informed the court that he had a large number of witnesses and a great deal of work was yet to be done. The applicant’s counsel gave notice of a potential abuse argument arising from the deaths of two of his witnesses. The judge fixed a timetable for further proceedings, including the lodging of an amended “section 11 statement” by the prosecution and reply by the applicant. The matter was listed for a hearing in [DATE_TIME]. The prosecution served the amended statement in [DATE_TIME]. At the hearing on [DATE_TIME] it was agreed to seek suitable dates in [DATE_TIME].

At a directions hearing on [DATE_TIME] the applicant’s counsel again raised issues relating to the volume of work and requested until [DATE_TIME] to respond to the prosecution’s “section 11 statement”. The judge extended the deadline to [DATE_TIME] and ordered that the prosecution serve any further response within [DATE_TIME]. A procedural hearing was agreed for [DATE_TIME]. The judge further extended the deadline for the confiscation hearing on the grounds of “exceptional circumstances”, stating that this was “a wholly exceptional case”.

At the procedural hearing on [DATE_TIME] the applicant proposed [DATE_TIME] for the substantive confiscation hearing and assured the judge that the hearing would not last longer than a week. The judge was scheduled to start a complex trial on [DATE_TIME] to last until [DATE_TIME]. He therefore listed the applicant’s case for [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the parties appeared before the judge. The applicant’s counsel informed the judge that, contrary to previous advice to the court, [DATE_TIME] would be insufficient for the substantive hearing as he now wished to call more witnesses than had originally been indicated. The judge’s other commitments precluded a rescheduled hearing taking place before [DATE_TIME] and counsel could not agree on dates after [DATE_TIME]. The judge decided to keep the hearing fixed for [DATE_TIME] to clarify the situation as to dates. The matter was further adjourned at hearings that took place in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. The substantive hearing was listed for [DATE_TIME], with a time estimate of [DATE_TIME], but in fact lasted [DATE_TIME] from [DATE_TIME].

The judge delivered his ruling on the confiscation on [DATE_TIME]. He identified the total amount of the applicant’s benefit from criminal conduct as GBP 1,840,563. He found the principal realisable asset to be a farm, which was valued at GBP 690,000. A confiscation order was made, with a [DATE_TIME] term of imprisonment to be served consecutive to the main sentence in default of payment. In his judgment, the judge also addressed the question of delay, noting that the delay incurred resulted partly from the applicant’s desire to challenge the jurisdiction of the court, partly from his appeal to the Court of Appeal and partly from his decision to change his legal representatives.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the judge to vary the confiscation order and reopen his findings on the delay issue on the basis of the judgment of this Court in [PERSON] and [PERSON] v. [LOCATION], no. [PHONE_NUMBER], [DATE_TIME]. The judge declined, noting that it was now for the applicant to seek other remedies.

C. Proceedings before the Court of Appeal

The applicant applied, out of [PERSON] to the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal the confiscation order. He argued, first, that the judge had erred in including the current value of the farm within the benefit figure of the proceeds of drug trafficking; and, secondly, that the delay in the disposal of the confiscation proceedings had breached his right to a fair trial and to a trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

An oral hearing took place before the full court to decide upon both leave to appeal and the merits on [DATE_TIME]. The Court of Appeal granted leave to appeal but dismissed the appeal itself, upholding the confiscation order and finding no violation of Article 6 § 1. As regards the delay complaint, the court considered the whole period from the applicant’s arrest in [DATE_TIME] to the making of the confiscation order in [DATE_TIME]. It indicated that the delay: “3. ... raises a prima facie case of a significant breach of Article 6. Unless there is a satisfactory explanation for it, it is a chronology which is way, way below the standards which are expected and achieved in the courts of this country. ...

... We start with the proposition that the passage of such a length of time as we have described calls for the most careful investigation and detailed justification. It is simply on the face of it well beyond acceptable.”

The court found that the period from the applicant’s arrest in [DATE_TIME] to the conclusion of his first trial on [DATE_TIME] was wholly unexceptional and reasonable. As to the period between the discharge of the jury in the first trial to the conclusion of the second trial in [DATE_TIME], a period of [DATE_TIME], the court accepted that the abandonment of the first trial was the fault of the prosecution, noting: “11. ... The trial had to start all over again. It was not concluded by conviction at [DATE_TIME] second trial until [DATE_TIME]. There is thus a period of [DATE_TIME] from [DATE_TIME] until [DATE_TIME] which was an unnecessary delay attributable to the error, although in good faith, made on behalf of the prosecution by some junior clerk. That period is therefore potentially available to be considered as the responsibility of the State.”

The court then examined the delay from [DATE_TIME] second trial in [DATE_TIME] until [DATE_TIME], when the House of Lords’ judgment in the jurisdiction appeals was handed down. It observed that at the outset of this period, the confiscation proceedings were moving in good time. The court considered that there would have been a hearing of the confiscation question in [DATE_TIME], if that probable timetable had not been overtaken by the applicant’s challenge to the court’s jurisdiction, of which the court noted;. “14. ... He was entitled to do so. The issue was raised before the trial judge in the early part of [DATE_TIME] ... The controversy as to the correct construction of the confiscation legislation was not resolved until the decision of the House of Lords in R v Bullen and [PERSON] ... In fact the question raised and decided went further than simply the confiscation legislation. It bore on a broader question of when technical failure to abide exactly by prescribed procedure has the effect of nullifying the subsequent actions of courts which is, of course, a very large general question.” The Court of Appeal considered that it was in the applicant’s interests to await the eventual authoritative ruling of the House of Lords. It therefore concluded that the delay that arose in this respect could not be criticised.

In the period from [DATE_TIME] until the applicant abandoned his appeal against conviction in [DATE_TIME], the court considered that the delay was the result of the appeal lodged “long out of time”, noting: “17. ... Whilst an appeal against conviction was outstanding there could not of course sensibly be a confiscation hearing because if the defendant’s conviction disappeared so would any prospect of confiscation.” The court observed that the applicant had engaged a third counsel for the appeal, and pursued it on grounds that had never been supported by those who had conducted his trial. It further noted that the various grounds advanced by the applicant fell away one by one over that period, but one of them remained and was not finally laid to rest until [DATE_TIME]. The court concluded: “19. ... The simple fact is that the appeal on this ground, as on the others, had always been without any proper basis or merit. It is this additional period to which we referred prospectively earlier on as an example of the defendant taking the course that he is quite entitled to do – leaving no legal stone unturned – but adding to the passage of time as a result. We are satisfied that nothing in that period can be called unreasonable delay attributable to the act or omission of the State.”

As regards the period [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME], when the confiscation order was eventually made, the Court of Appeal noted that the parties had returned promptly to the Crown Court for the resumption of the confiscation issue within a fortnight of the abandonment of the appeal against conviction. It was apparent at the hearing of [DATE_TIME] that the prosecution was pressing for a short timetable. The applicant’s representatives, on the other hand, wanted a longer timetable and were seeking additional time on the grounds that they had an enormous volume of work and would be calling a large number of witnesses, and might even be mounting an abuse argument on the grounds that some potential witnesses had died. Hearings were adjourned owing to the applicant’s applications. Although the Court of Appeal did not blame the applicant for his conduct, the court made it clear that any additional passage of time as a result of that conduct was not attributable to any act of the State. It observed in particular that: “20. ... At one such hearing, in [DATE_TIME], the defendant through his lawyers indicated that there would be no less than 49 witnesses necessary to be examined at the confiscation hearing ... [that] was eventually set down for [DATE_TIME], taking into account the potentially large number of witnesses and time that would be needed. At that stage the estimate, which according to English practice will have been an estimate contributed to by both parties, was [DATE_TIME]. That is a very long time for a confiscation hearing but if the time has to be found it has to be found. However, that date had to be broken on the application of the defendant because they assured the judge that they had so many witnesses to call that in fact [DATE_TIME] would be needed, that is [DATE_TIME], to hear the confiscation question. In the end, the defendant called five (not 49) witnesses and one of those was himself.”

The court commented on the time taken by the Crown Court judge to deliver his ruling (some four and a half months after the conclusion of the confiscation hearing) as follows: “22. ... We do not doubt that that will be attributable to the demands made on the judges at the Central Criminal Court, but it is too long and that period, or at least part of it, is no doubt the responsibility of the State. Judgments of this kind ought to be delivered within, at the very least, [DATE_TIME].”

Looking at the passage of time as a whole, the court concluded that there had not been in the applicant’s case unreasonable delay attributable to the acts of the State. The court also considered the impact of the passage of time upon the applicant, and acknowledged that he and his wife lived throughout this time with the uncertainty of whether they would lose his family home. However, given that his assets remained the same throughout the whole period and that he continued to enjoy his home which might have otherwise been taken from him earlier, the court had very little doubt about where the balance of advantage lay. It concluded: “25. The reality of this case is that this was a defendant of resourceful approach who deployed every possible legal stratagem to delay the confiscation process. He cannot now be heard to say that as a result of his having succeeded in delaying it, it has become unfair for the confiscation order to proceed. If there had been unreasonable delay attributable to the State, in the absence of any possible damage to the defendant beyond the very limited uncertainty that we have mentioned we are quite satisfied that this could not possibly have been a case in which the appropriate remedy would have been a stay of the confiscation process for abuse of process. There would simply have been nothing remotely unfair about the defendant eventually having to disgorge the confiscation which was the consequence of his offending. The appropriate remedy would, hypothetically, as it seems to us, have been a declaration. But that does not in the end arise. It follows that the substantive ground ... in relation to Article 6 fails.”

Since the lodging of his application to this Court, a further judgment has been handed down by the High Court on [DATE_TIME], substantially reducing the amount of assets payable under the confiscation order (CPS v Piper [[DATE_TIME]] EWHC 3570 (Admin)).

train_texts: The case was brought under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his case had not been heard within a reasonable time. The application was granted priority pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. The case was transferred from the Fourth Section to the Third Section. It was ruled inadmissible on [DATE_TIME] and the case was dismissed. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The decision was made to dismiss the case on the same date the application was declared admissible. The applicant filed an application for distribution of the estate of [PERSON] The estate consisted of three plots of land and a house and had so far been held in individual shares. On [DATE_TIME] the Kraków District Court gave a decision (postanowienie) distributing the estate. On an extraordinary appeal lodged by the Minister of Justice, the Supreme Court partly quashed the decisions of both lower courts, and remitted the case to the District Court. The subsequent proceedings concerned solely the amount of payments for the respective shares in the estate, and were adjourned until at least 1 [DATED_TIME]. The applicant requested the court to enter a warning in the land register about the proceedings related to the estate. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant challenged the presiding judge. The applicant filed further pleadings with the court. The District Court held a hearing and heard the expert. The hearing was adjourned at the petitioners’ request. The petitioners agreed with the conclusions of the expert report in principle, but requested that a further supplementary report be prepared. They agreed that this should take place. The court ruled that an interim order should be issued for the hearing to be held. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the hearing was not necessary. The applicant appealed against the decision of [DATE_TIME]. The applicant rectified procedural defects in his appeal and paid the fee due for lodging the appeal. The Kraków Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. On the same date, on the joint request of the parties, the court stayed the proceedings. The court heard evidence from two witnesses and imposed a fine on another witness who did not appear at the hearing. The case file was received at the registry of the District Court of Krakowsk. The applicant asked the court to obtain a report from another expert. Two experts refused to prepare a report. On an unspecified date expert [PERSON] agreed to prepare an expert report. The court dismissed the applicant’s claim for the maintenance expenses and for the house because these issues had already been determined in the decision of [DATE_TIME]. The court based its decision exclusively on the report of an expert, which assessed the market value of the estate. It regarded the reports prepared by experts [PERSON] and J.W. outdated. The applicant appealed and asked the court to exempt him from a fee due for lodging an appeal. The District Court gave a decision and ordered S.Z. to pay off the applicants’ share in the estate, but it dismissed the claims for the upkeep of the house and maintenance expenses. The applicant challenged the impartiality of two judges of the Regional Court. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested to be exempted from a court fee due for lodging a cassation appeal. The applicant paid the fee himself. The Supreme Court heard, and dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeals. The case file was transferred to the Supreme Court. It was adjourned until the latter date due to the absence of a witness. The court closed examination of the case and adjourned delivery of a decision until the end of the year. The judge ruled that the appeal was not necessary to be heard. The appeal was dismissed and the case was closed.

PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 52518/99) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant alleged that his case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. On [DATE_TIME] the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint about the length of the proceedings to the Government. On the same date the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. The application was granted priority pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of Court.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1).This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section .

By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the application admissible.

Subsequently, the case was transferred to [LOCATION].

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION], [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the Chrzanów District Court ([PERSON]) gave a decision (postanowienie) declaring that, under the will of [PERSON] (the applicant’s mother-in-law), her estate be inherited by her three daughters [LOCATION], [NRP] and [PERSON] (the applicant’s wife) and by her granddaughter ([PERSON]). On [DATE_TIME] [LOCATION] (Sąd Rejonowy) declared that the applicant had inherited the estate of his late wife.

1. Facts prior to 1 [DATE_TIME]

On [DATE_TIME] [LOCATION], [NRP] and [PERSON] (“the petitioners”) filed with the Kraków District Court ([LOCATION]) an application for distribution of the estate of [PERSON] The estate consisted of three plots of land and a house and had so far been held in individual shares. The applicant was a party to these proceedings as a successor to his wife.

On [DATE_TIME] the Kraków District Court gave a decision (postanowienie) distributing the estate. Upon the applicant’s appeal, on [DATE_TIME] the Kraków Regional Court ([PERSON]) partly amended the first-instance decision.

The case originated in an application (no. 40694/98) against [LOCATION] lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Zenon Sobański (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant was represented by Mr [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION], [LOCATION]. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], Government's Agent.

The applicant alleged in particular, that the civil proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.

The application was transmitted to the Court on [DATE_TIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11).

The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the application partly inadmissible.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section.

By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. The applicant, but not the Government, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION]. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant, following clashes with the police during anticommunist demonstrations, was put by the police in their van and beaten. He was seriously injured. On [DATE_TIME] he was discharged from hospital. A brain injury, post-traumatic epilepsy and permanent brain damage were diagnosed. Since then he has remained under permanent care in a psychiatric clinic.

By a judgment of [DATE_TIME], the Warsaw Regional Court granted the applicant compensation for damage to his health and held that a [DATE_TIME] supplementary pension be paid by the police – the State Treasury. The court observed that the applicant had lost the capacity to work and was disabled in the so-called second degree (an intermediate degree of disability).

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was granted the first degree status of disability (serious disability).

In [DATE_TIME] the [DATE_TIME] supplementary pension was increased to 100 PLN as a result of a settlement between the parties.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant's father lodged a claim with the Warsaw Regional Court, in which he requested an increase in his son's [DATE_TIME] pension. On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Regional Court remitted the case to the Warsaw District Court. Subsequently, six hearings were held in the case. On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing. The defendant's lawyer asked for an adjournment in order to reach a friendly settlement.

On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing. The applicant increased the amount of the claim. The court decided to request certain information from the applicant's former employer. On [DATE_TIME] the court obtained the requested information.

On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing. The applicant increased the amount of the claim. The court decided to request the psychiatric clinic for some additional information on the applicant's health. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant's lawyer specified the claim. He requested the court to appoint an expert to give a report on the applicant's health.

On [DATE_TIME] the next hearing was held. It was decided to request the psychiatric clinic to expedite the preparation of the requested documents.

On [DATE_TIME] the court held its next hearing and interviewed witnesses. The applicant further specified the claim.

On [DATE_TIME] a hearing was held. The defendant contested the amount of the applicant's claim. The court decided to request the applicant's former employer to submit certain information. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant increased his claim. Taking into account the value of the claim, on [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the court to remit the case to the Regional Court. On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw District Court remitted the case to the Warsaw Regional Court, as the latter had become competent following the increase of the applicant's claim. Subsequently, on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the defendant and the applicant submitted pleadings to the court.

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the court not to schedule any hearings in the period from 1 until [DATE_TIME]. In [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the court not to schedule any hearings from 1 until [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant increased the claim.

On [DATE_TIME] the parties asked for an adjournment in order to reach an out-of-court settlement. Their negotiations subsequently failed. By pleadings of [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the applicant further specified his claim. On [DATE_TIME] the court requested the applicant's former employer to submit certain documents. The documents were submitted on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the hearing was adjourned to give the applicant [DATE_TIME] to submit his comments on the documents received by the court on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the applicant specified his claim. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant complained to the Supreme Court about the length of the proceedings. On [DATE_TIME] he was informed that the case had been placed under the administrative supervision of the President of the Warsaw Regional Court.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant lodged a motion with the Warsaw Regional Court challenging the presiding judge for an alleged lack of impartiality. This motion was dismissed on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the court received requested information from the applicant's former employer. On [DATE_TIME] the expert submitted a report ordered by the court in [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant's lawyer requested the court not to schedule any hearings in [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the court requested the parties to submit their comments on the expert report within [DATE_TIME] time-limit. On [DATE_TIME] the defendant informed the court that he agreed with the conclusions of the report. On [DATE_TIME] the court once more requested the applicant to submit his comments. Apparently, further questions were put to the expert. On [DATE_TIME] the expert submitted to the court the supplementary report. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant lodged his objections against the report.

On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing. The applicant requested the court to appoint a new expert. He once more challenged the expert opinion. The court refused and closed the hearings in the case.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant increased and modified his claim to a very significant extent.

On [DATE_TIME] the court accordingly re-opened the proceedings. The court also gave an interlocutory decision that a certain sum be paid [DATE_TIME] to the applicant in order to secure his claim.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant submitted motions as to the evidence to be taken. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant submitted a new proposal for calculating the amount of the pension. On [DATE_TIME] the defendant opposed that new proposal. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant increased his claim.

On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing.

By a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the applicant's claim was partly dismissed and partly allowed. The judgment was served on the applicant [DATE_TIME]. The applicant appealed. By an order of [DATE_TIME], he was requested to submit certain copies of documents for his appeal. This order was left by the postman at the applicant's door. Later, the post office returned it to the court marked “apartment closed”.

On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Regional Court rejected the applicant' s appeal for failure to comply with its order of [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant complained to the Warsaw Appeal Court. On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Court of Appeal remitted the case to the Warsaw Regional Court and ordered the court to clarify whether the applicant wished to challenge the decision of [DATE_TIME], or to lodge a request in order to reinstate the time-limit for submitting the requested documents.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant appealed against the decision of [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Regional Court ordered the applicant to pay a court fee of 50 PLN for the procedural appeal, which the applicant did on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant received an order dated [DATE_TIME] summoning him to pay 50 PLN in court fees. The applicant requested a meeting with the President of the Civil Section on [DATE_TIME] in order to clarify what the court fee was for. The meeting did not take place as the President was absent on the date which had been fixed. The President apologised in a letter of [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the applicant specified his claim.

By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the decision of [DATE_TIME] and rejected his appeal on the merits of the case for failure to comply with the procedural requirements. The court informed the applicant that he could lodge a request to reinstate the time-limit for submitting the documents requested by the court.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the court to appoint a lawyer under the legal aid scheme with a view to lodging a cassation appeal against the decision of [DATE_TIME]. He lodged also a “personal” cassation appeal. On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Court of Appeal allowed this request, but the lawyer was not appointed until [DATE_TIME].

In the meantime, on [DATE_TIME] the Court of Appeal rejected the cassation appeal against the decision of 29 [DATE_TIME] for not having been presented by a lawyer as required by law. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant's lawyer lodged an appeal against the decision of [DATE_TIME] with the Supreme Court in order to reinstate the time-limit for lodging the cassation appeal. The cassation appeal itself was submitted to the Supreme Court on [DATE_TIME].

By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Supreme Court quashed the decision of [DATE_TIME] for having been reached without due consideration to the applicant's pending legal aid application.

On [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] the applicant specified the claim.

On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Court of Appeal reinstated the time-limit for lodging the cassation appeal against the procedural decisions of 29 [DATE_TIME] and of [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Supreme Court quashed the decisions of 29 [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] for procedural defects.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant increased his claim.

By a letter of [DATE_TIME], the Warsaw Court of Appeal informed the applicant that the next hearing in the appellate proceedings would be held on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Warsaw Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the judgment of [DATE_TIME]. The judgment was served on the applicant on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant's lawyer lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. On [DATE_TIME] the court rejected the cassation appeal, considering that it had not been shown that arguable grounds existed which would justify the examination of the appeal.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 63477/00) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Court decided to adjourn the applicant’s complaint in connection with his claims for widows’ benefits, relating to discrimination suffered by him during the period after the date on which he lodged his claim. The applicant was represented by [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [Person] of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, [ LOCATION]. The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION]. His wife died on [Dates] 1997‑1999 leaving four children. He applied for benefits equivalent to those to which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled. He was told that he had no right of appeal since his claim had not been considered by a decision maker. The applicant received child benefit in the sum of GBP 150.20 per month. The case was heard by the Chamber to which the case had been allocated. The Chamber decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

The decision was appealed to the European Court of Human Rights, which is due to make a decision on the matter in two weeks' time. The case is set to continue until a decision is made on the appeal's appeal. The German government says it will continue to defend the right of the citizens of Germany to have their right to access the water resources of their homes. The applicants' predecessors filed a request for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) as the District Authority failed to decide within the statutory [DATE_TIME] time-limit. The Municipalities applied for an ex post permission. The Federal Minister for Agriculture and Forestry (Bundesminister für Land- und Forstwirtschaft) allowed the appeal. The Regional Governor had to take a decision on the merits on the appeal against the Regional Governor's decision. The District Authority dismissed the request for compensation and ordered the Municipalities to take specific steps to ensure the water supply of the fishing farm before [Date_TIME]. The applicants' water rights had been prejudiced by the regulation works. The ownership on the fishing farm was transferred to the applicants and thereby, they became parties to the proceedings at issue. The applicants lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court as well as with the Administrative Court. The Federal Minister dismissed the appeal and confirmed the Regional Governor's decision of [DATE_TIME]. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador [PERSON], Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

The applicants were born in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME], respectively, and live in [LOCATION], [LOCATION].

The applicants run a fishing farm in Schalchen since [DATE_TIME]. Before that date the parents of the first applicant had run the fishing farm.

[DATE_TIME] the Braunau River Engineering Directorate (Flussbauleitung) carried out regulation works on a small river in the vicinity of the applicants' estate without permission under the Water Act (Wasserrechtsgesetz [DATE_TIME]).

In [DATE_TIME] the former owners of the estate requested the Braunau District Authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft) to order the Municipalities of Mattighofen and [PERSON] (“the Municipalities”) to re-establish the former state of the river bed maintaining that the regulation works had damaged the well which supplied their fishing farm with water. They submitted that the original capacity of the well had been 800 litres of water per second. After the regulation of the river the capacity of the well had been reduced to 100 litres of water per second. This constituted an interference with their water-rights. In case that the regulation could not be reversed they requested that the Municipalities be ordered to take other steps to ensure the water supply of the fishing farm.

On [DATE_TIME] the District Authority dismissed this request.

On [DATE_TIME] the Upper Austria Regional Governor allowed the appeal and remitted the case to the District Authority to decide on the request.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicants' predecessors filed a request for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) as the District Authority failed to decide within the statutory [DATE_TIME] time-limit. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Governor dismissed this request.

On [DATE_TIME] they filed again a request for transfer of jurisdiction and the Regional Governor again dismissed this request. The applicants' predecessors filed an appeal against this decision.

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Minister for Agriculture and Forestry (Bundesminister für Land- und Forstwirtschaft) allowed the appeal as a consequence of which the Regional Governor had to take a decision on the merits.

On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Governor ordered the Municipalities to ask for an ex post permission of the regulation works which had already been carried out or to re-establish the former state of the river.

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Minister dismissed the Municipalities' appeal.

Subsequently, on [DATE_TIME] the Municipalities applied for an ex post permission. On [DATE_TIME] the District Authority held a hearing. At this hearing the applicants' predecessors requested that the Municipalities be ordered to pay compensation as they had suffered prejudice caused by the regulation works.

On [DATE_TIME] the District Authority granted the ex post permission and ordered the Municipalities to take specific steps to ensure the water supply of the fishing farm before [DATE_TIME]. The District Authority dismissed the request for compensation.

On [DATE_TIME] Regional Governor dismissed the applicants' predecessors' appeal and found that their water rights were not violated by the granted permission.

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Minister rejected the applicants' predecessors' appeal as belated. Subsequently, they lodged a request for leave to appeal out of time (Wiedereinsetzung in den [PERSON] Stand).

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Minister granted this request and, consequently, had to take a decision on the merits on the appeal against the Regional Governor's decision of [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the ownership on the fishing farm was transferred to the applicants and thereby, they became parties to the proceedings at issue.

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Minister dismissed the appeal and confirmed the Regional Governor's decision of [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Administrative Court, upon a complaint lodged by the applicants, quashed this decision and found that the administrative authorities had not properly decided whether the applicants' water rights had been prejudiced by the regulation works.

Subsequently, on [DATE_TIME], the Federal Minister remitted the case to the Regional Governor and on [DATE_TIME] the Regional Governor remitted the case to the District Authority.
