PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Mrs [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant was represented by the Aire Centre, an NGO situated in [LOCATION]. The Danish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and their Co-Agent, Mrs [PERSON], from the Ministry of Justice.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that the [NRP] authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in [LOCATION] was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention.

On [DATE_TIME] the acting President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1).

On [DATE_TIME] the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed First Section.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [LOCATION] on [DATE_TIME] as the youngest of five siblings. Currently she lives in [LOCATION].

From [DATE_TIME] the applicant lived with her family in [LOCATION].

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant’s father and a sister were granted asylum in [LOCATION].

Having been granted a residence permit in [DATE_TIME], on [DATE_TIME] the applicant, who at the relevant time was [DATE_TIME], her mother and three siblings joined them. [DATE_TIME], the applicant’s parents divorced. The parents maintained joint custody of the applicant, who lived with her mother. From [DATE_TIME] until [DATE_TIME], the applicant attended various schools, some of which expelled her due to disciplinary problems.

The applicant also had difficulties with her parents, who disapproved of certain aspects of her behaviour. Consequently, in [DATE_TIME], when the applicant was [DATE_TIME], her father decided to take her to [LOCATION] to take care of her paternal grandmother, who was living at the [PERSON] refugee camp in north‑eastern [LOCATION]. It appears that the applicant’s mother did not want her to go but reluctantly agreed on the understanding that it would be a short trip. It also appears that the applicant believed that she was going on a short trip to visit her grandmother.

When the applicant’s father returned to [LOCATION], he was summoned for an interview with the Immigration Service on [DATE_TIME] because the latter had been informed that he, who had been recognised as a refugee, had visited his country of origin. On [DATE_TIME] the Immigration Service (Udlændingeservice) took the stand that the applicant’s father’s residence permit had not lapsed. In that connection, the applicant’s father was advised on the regulation regarding lapse of residence permits.

On [DATE_TIME], [DATE_TIME] before the applicant turned [DATE_TIME], she contacted the Danish Embassy in [LOCATION] with a view to returning to live with her mother and siblings in [LOCATION]. Her father had joined her in [LOCATION] to help her submit the application for family reunification. He also remarried in [LOCATION] at the relevant time. An interview was conducted with the help of an English/[NRP] interpreter although it was stated that the applicant spoke [NRP]. The applicant explained that she had taken care of her grandmother, who had fallen seriously ill, until some of the grandmother’s children had arrived from [LOCATION] to take over the care of their mother.

In a letter of [DATE_TIME] to the Immigration Service the applicant’s mother stated, inter alia, that at the relevant time it had been decided temporarily to send the applicant to [LOCATION] where the family had a network so that she could attend school and that the applicant had been living with her father’s friends.

On [DATE_TIME] the Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from [LOCATION] for [DATE_TIME]; because she had not contacted the Immigration Service until [DATE_TIME]; and because there was no information indicating that she could not have contacted the authorities in due time. They also considered that the applicant was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act, in force at the relevant time, since the applicant was [DATE_TIME] and the said provision only extended a right to family reunification to children below [DATE_TIME]. Finally, it found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permit under section 9 c, subsection 1, of the Aliens Act. It noted in that connection that the applicant had not seen her mother for [DATE_TIME]; that it had been the latter’s voluntary decision to send the applicant to [LOCATION]; that she could still enjoy family life with her mother to the same extent as before; that she had stayed with the grandmother; and that except for the grandmother’s age, there was no information that the applicant could not continue to live with her or the grandmother’s children.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant appealed against the decision and maintained that it had not been her decision to leave the country; that from the refugee camp where she lived with her grandmother she was not able herself to go to [LOCATION]; and that during her stay outside [LOCATION] she had not stayed in her country of origin.

According to the applicant, in [DATE_TIME] she re-entered [LOCATION] clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the [NRP] authorities were aware of this.

On [DATE_TIME] the Immigration Service received a questionnaire from the applicant dated [DATE_TIME] used for requests for exemption from the authorities revoking a residence permit despite a stay outside [LOCATION] for a certain period. It was partly filled out and stated, inter alia, that it had been the applicant’s parents’ decision that she should leave [LOCATION] at the relevant time; that the applicant spoke [NRP], but could not read or write the language; that she spoke the language of the country in which she was currently residing, but that she could not read or write that language either; and that she was very afraid and could not reside in her country of origin as there was unrest. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to [LOCATION], but her signature was dated as set out above in [LOCATION], [LOCATION]. It was also stated that her sister had assisted her in answering the questionnaire.

On [DATE_TIME] the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs (Ministeriet for flygtninge, indvandrere og integration) upheld the decision by the Migration Service of [DATE_TIME]. It stated among other things: “... The Ministry emphasises that there is no information available of any circumstances that would lead to [the applicant’s] residence permit being deemed not to have lapsed ... [the applicant’s] parents did not apply for retention of [her] residence permit before she left, and neither she nor her parents contacted the immigration authorities during her stay abroad, and it has not been substantiated that illness or other unforeseen events prevented such contact. Thus, the Ministry finds that the illness of [the applicant’s] grandmother did not prevent [the applicant] or her parents from contacting the immigration authorities. Although the distance from [LOCATION] to [LOCATION] is significant [485 km] and it can be assumed that [the applicant] did not have the means to travel to [LOCATION], the Ministry finds that these circumstances did not prevent [the applicant’s] parents from contacting the immigration authorities before [the applicant’s] departure, which was planned. The fact that [the applicant] stayed in [LOCATION] and not in [LOCATION] does not change the fact that [she] has resided abroad for [DATE_TIME]. It is stated for the record that it was not [the applicant’s] decision to leave [LOCATION] and stay away so long. The ministry finds that this will not lead to a different outcome of the case as [the applicant’s] parents had custody over her at the time of her departure ... they could thus lawfully make decisions about [her] personal circumstances...”

Upon request from the applicant, who was represented by counsel, on [DATE_TIME] the Immigration Service brought the case concerning section 17 and section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act before the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret), before which the case was decided on the documents submitted, without any parties being summoned. On [DATE_TIME] it found against the applicant. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children [DATE_TIME] instead of [DATE_TIME] in order to discourage the practice of some parents of sending their children on “re-upbringing trips” for extended periods of time to be “re-educated” in a manner their parents consider more consistent with their ethnic origins. It was preferable in the legislator’s view for foreign minors living in [LOCATION] to arrive as early as possible and spend as many of [DATE_TIME] as possible in [LOCATION]. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention as invoked by the applicant.

The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark ([PERSON]), henceforth the High Court, before which the applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in [LOCATION]. On [DATE_TIME] the High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. By way of introduction, it stated that according to section 52 of the Aliens Act, it could not review a final administrative decision of refusal of a residence permit under section 9c, subsection 1, of the Aliens Act. As to section 9, subsection 1 (ii) it confirmed that the applicant failed to fulfil the conditions. It took into account that the applicant’s parents had sent her voluntarily to [LOCATION] to live with family for an indefinite period; that the applicant was [DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME], when in [DATE_TIME] she applied to re-enter [LOCATION]; that her father visited her during her stay in [LOCATION]; and that her mother would also be able to visit the applicant in [LOCATION] to enjoy family life there.

Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on [DATE_TIME].

By letter of [DATE_TIME] the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave [LOCATION] pursuant to section 30 of the Alien’s Act and the possibility of submitting an application for asylum under section 7 of the Aliens Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police.

So far the applicant has not applied for asylum.

It originated in an application (no. [DATE_TIME]) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on [DATE_TIME] by a [NRP] citizen, Mr [PERSON]. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30).

[LOCATION] (no. 31/[PHONE_NUMBER]) should be heard by the same Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6). On [DATE_TIME], in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mrs [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON], Mr [PERSON] and Mr [PERSON] (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43).

As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), Mr [PERSON], acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and [DATE_TIME]). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial on [DATE_TIME] and the Government’s memorial on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the Government submitted their written reply to the applicant’s claims for just satisfaction under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. On [DATE_TIME] the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would not submit written observations in reply.

[DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] he stood trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting in [LOCATION].

This was not disputed by the applicant’s counsel, who, moreover, was unable to give any indication as to how Mrs [PERSON]’s evidence could be affected by her earlier presence in court. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 68354/01) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant association alleged that the [NRP] courts' decisions forbidding it to continue exhibiting a painting by [PERSON] had violated its right to freedom of expression. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the application admissible. The painting shows a former general secretary of the Austrian Freedom Party (FPÖ) in sexual positions. The eyes of some of the persons portrayed were hidden under black bars. Mr [PERSON] brought proceedings under section 78 of the Copyright Act against the applicant association, seeking an injunction. He argued that the painting debased him and his political activities and made statements as to his allegedly loose sexual life. The black eye-bars did not prevent him from being recognised, because he was shown together with two other FPÖ politicians. He remained recognisable even after the incident of [DATE_TIME], which had further increased the publicity given to the painting. The Vienna Commercial Court (Handelsgericht) dismissed Mr [PERSON]'s action. The court further found that it could be ruled out that the painting had adversely affected the claimant or divulged information about his private life. The right of the applicant association to freedom of artistic expression outweighed the claimant's personal interests. The painting showed numerous other persons, among them friends and benefactors of the painter, and also representatives of the FPÖ party, which had always strongly criticised the painter's work. The Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), after having held an oral hearing, granted an appeal on points of law and fact. The limits of artistic freedom were exceeded when the image of a person was substantially deformed by wholly imaginary elements without it being evident that the picture aimed at satire or any other form of exaggeration. The painting in the present case was not intended to be a parable or even an exaggerated criticism conveying a basic message. It therefore did not fall within the scope of Article 10 of the Convention, but in fact constituted a debasement of Mr [PERSON]'s public standing. The Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the applicant association as it did not concern a legal question of considerable interest. The Court of Appeal had not contradicted the documents contained in the court file and there was no need for a rectification.

test_texts:
PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 68354/01) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an association, [LOCATION] (“the applicant association”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant association was represented by Schönherr OEG, a law firm practising in [LOCATION]. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador [PERSON], Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs.

The applicant association alleged that the [NRP] courts' decisions forbidding it to continue exhibiting a painting by [PERSON] had violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention.

The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Court declared the application admissible.

Neither the applicant association nor the Government filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

Vereinigung Bildender Künstler Wiener Secession is an association of artists with its seat in the Secession building in [LOCATION]. The Secession, an independent gallery, is devoted entirely to exhibitions of contemporary art. One of the basic objectives of the association is to present current developments in [NRP] and international art, and to cultivate an openness to experimentation.

[DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME] the applicant association held an exhibition on its premises. The exhibition, entitled “The century of artistic freedom” (“Das Jahrhundert künstlerischer Freiheit”), was intended as part of the celebrations of the association's 100th anniversary. Among the works to be shown was a painting entitled “Apocalypse”, which had been produced for the occasion by the [NRP] painter [PERSON]. The painting, measuring 450 cm by 360 cm, showed a collage of various public figures, such as [PERSON], the [NRP] cardinal [PERSON] and the former head of the Austrian Freedom Party (FPÖ) Mr [PERSON], in sexual positions. While the naked bodies of these figures were painted, the heads and faces were depicted using blown-up photos taken from newspapers. The eyes of some of the persons portrayed were hidden under black bars. Among these persons was Mr [PERSON], a former general secretary of the FPÖ until [DATE_TIME], who at the time of the events was a member of the National Assembly (Nationalratsabgeordneter), a mandate he held until [DATE_TIME]. Mr [PERSON] was shown gripping the ejaculating penis of Mr [PERSON] while at the same time being touched by two other FPÖ politicians and ejaculating on Mother [PERSON].

The exhibition, for which admission was charged, was open to the public.

On [DATE_TIME], while the exhibition was in progress, the [NRP] newspaper [PERSON] bristled at the above painting's portayal of “group sexual situations with Bishop [PERSON] and Mother [PERSON]”.

On [DATE_TIME] the painting was damaged by a visitor, who covered with red paint the part which showed, among others, Mr [PERSON]. As a consequence of this incident the entire painted body of Mr [PERSON] and part of his face were covered with red paint.

Several [NRP] newspapers reported on this event and also published pictures of the painting.

On [DATE_TIME] Mr [PERSON] brought proceedings under section 78 of the Copyright Act (Urheberrechtsgesetz) against the applicant association, seeking an injunction prohibiting it from exhibiting and publishing the painting. He further requested compensation in the amount of 20,000 [NRP] schillings (ATS – 1,453.46 euros (EUR)). He argued that the painting, showing him in sexual positions with several persons, debased him and his political activities and made statements as to his allegedly loose sexual life (lotterhaftes [PERSON]). The black eye-bars did not prevent him from being recognised, because he was shown together with two other FPÖ politicians. He remained recognisable even after the incident of [DATE_TIME], which had further increased the publicity given to the painting. Furthermore, there was a danger of recurrence as after the present exhibition the painting was due to be shown at another exhibition in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the Vienna Commercial Court (Handelsgericht) dismissed Mr [PERSON]'s action. It noted that it had initially been intended to show the exhibition in [LOCATION], [LOCATION] and [LOCATION] as well; now the intention was to close down the exhibition. The court further found that it could be ruled out that the painting had adversely affected the claimant or divulged information about his private life, as the painting, which resembled a comic strip (“comixartig”), obviously did not represent reality. However, a painting showing the claimant in such an intimate position could, regardless of its relation to reality, still have a degrading and personally debasing effect. In the present case, however, the right of the applicant association to freedom of artistic expression outweighed Mr [PERSON]'s personal interests. When balancing the latter's interests against the interests of the applicant association, the court had regard in particular to the fact that the exhibition was dedicated to the association's artistic spectrum over [DATE_TIME], which included the work of the [NRP] painter [PERSON]. It further noted that the painting showed numerous other persons, among them friends and benefactors of the painter, and also representatives of the FPÖ party, which had always strongly criticised Mr [PERSON]'s work.

The painting in question could therefore be seen as a kind of counter-attack ([PERSON]). In any event, Mr [PERSON]'s picture constituted only a rather small part of the painting and was therefore not striking. The court further added that there appeared to be no danger of recurrence ([PERSON]) as the painting had been partly covered by red paint and Mr [PERSON] was therefore no longer recognisable on it.

On [DATE_TIME] the Vienna Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), after having held an oral hearing, granted an appeal on points of law and fact by Mr [PERSON], issued an injunction against the applicant association prohibiting it from continuing to display the painting at exhibitions, and ordered it to pay the costs incurred by Mr [PERSON] in the proceedings and ATS 20,000 (EUR 1,453.46), plus 4% interest with effect from [DATE_TIME], in compensation. It further allowed Mr [PERSON] to publish extracts of its judgment in two [NRP] newspapers. It noted that Mr [PERSON]'s picture was only partly covered by red paint, so that part of his face, the shape of his head and his hairstyle were still recognisable. The limits of artistic freedom were exceeded when the image of a person was substantially deformed by wholly imaginary elements without it being evident that the picture aimed at satire or any other form of exaggeration. The painting in the present case was not intended to be a parable or even an exaggerated criticism conveying a basic message, such as, for example, the statement that Mr [PERSON] had disregarded sexual decency and morals. It therefore did not fall within the scope of Article 10 of the Convention, but in fact constituted a debasement of Mr [PERSON]'s public standing ([NRP] öffentlichen [LOCATION]). The applicant association could not justify the exhibition of the painting under the artistic freedom protected by Article 17a of the Basic Law (Staatsgrundsgesetz). There was, furthermore, nothing to indicate that the applicant association would abstain from exhibiting the painting in the future, so that there was a danger of recurrence.

On [DATE_TIME] the Supreme Court ([PERSON]) rejected an appeal by the applicant association as it did not concern a legal question of considerable interest. It noted that the Court of Appeal had not questioned the fact that the painting fell within the scope of protection provided by Article 17a of the Basic Law but, weighing the guarantee of artistic freedom enshrined in that provision against Mr [PERSON]'s personal rights as protected by section 78 of the Copyright Act, had considered that the latter prevailed over the former because a picture of Mr [PERSON] had been used in a degrading and insulting manner. As to the question whether Mr [PERSON] could still be recognised despite the painting being covered with red paint, the Court of Appeal had not contradicted the documents contained in the court file and there was therefore no need for a rectification. It ordered the applicant association to pay the costs of the proceedings.

That decision was served on the applicant association's counsel on [DATE_TIME].

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 43626/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant complained, in particular, that he had been held in detention arbitrarily. The case was allocated to the Second Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed further written observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry. A forged identity card bearing the applicant’s photo was discovered, together with a sawn-off shotgun. The employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing. The Indictment Division of the Versailles Court of Appeal ordered further investigations to be made and appointed for that purpose the investigating judge at the [LOCATION] tribunal de grande instance who had previously been in charge of the investigation. The judge issued a warrant of commitment for armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence resulting in total unfitness for work. PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 43626/98) against [LOCATION] lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mrs [PERSON], of the Val-de-Marne Bar. The French Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], Director of Legal Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Relying on Article 5 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention, the applicant complained, in particular, that he had been held in detention arbitrarily in that he had been kept in custody even though the order extending his detention had expired.

The application was transmitted to the Court on [DATE_TIME], when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11).

The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

By a decision of [DATE_TIME] the Chamber declared the application partly admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry].

On [DATE_TIME] the Government, but not the applicant, filed further written observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

On [DATE_TIME] four armed robbers wearing masks entered the premises of a transport company which employed a number of inmates from Poissy Prison who were in semi-detention or on external work assignments. After locking the entire staff in the lavatories, they forced the company manager, whom they had taken hostage, to open the safe, from which they stole 120,000 French francs (FRF) in cash before making off. The investigators concentrated their inquiries on some of the prison inmates. One of them, G.D., had witnessed the offences and been threatened by the robbers.

On [DATE_TIME] the managing director of the company had a cheque stolen. The home of one of the company’s employees, [PERSON], was searched and a forged identity card bearing the applicant’s photo was discovered, together with a sawn-off shotgun. The employee admitted that he had provided the applicant with information to help him commit the armed robbery in return for the sum of FRF 10,000. He also stated that he had recognised the applicant while the offence was being committed despite the mask he had been wearing and that the applicant was the robber who had been carrying the sawn-off shotgun.

On [DATE_TIME] the investigating judge at the [LOCATION] tribunal de grande instance decided to have the applicant detained pending trial and issued a warrant of commitment for armed robbery, false imprisonment, and wounding with intent and wilful violence resulting in total unfitness for work for [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the investigating judge made an order extending detention for [DATE_TIME] from [DATE_TIME].

The applicant’s detention was twice extended for [DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME], on [DATE_TIME] from [DATE_TIME] onwards and on [DATE_TIME] from [DATE_TIME] onwards.

On [DATE_TIME] the investigating judge substituted for the charge of false imprisonment with voluntary release (an intermediate offence (délit)) the more serious one of false imprisonment (crime) and made a partial discharge order. In accordance with Article 181 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, he ordered that the file be transferred to the public prosecutor’s office at the Versailles Court of Appeal with a view to the Indictment Division indicting the applicant and committing him for trial at the Assize Court. That order was served on the applicant on [DATE_TIME].

In a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the Indictment Division of the Versailles Court of Appeal ordered further investigations to be made and appointed for that purpose the investigating judge at the [LOCATION] tribunal de grande instance who had previously been in charge of the investigation.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested that a bailiff be called on to record officially that his detention had become unlawful as the last order extending it, dated [DATE_TIME] and effective from [DATE_TIME] on [DATE_TIME] for [DATE_TIME] [DATE_TIME], had expired at [DATE_TIME] on [DATE_TIME].

In a formal demand for information ([PERSON]) addressed to the governor of [LOCATION] the bailiff asked to be sent the detention order by virtue of which the applicant was still being held in his prison. In reply he was told that the applicant was being detained under the transfer order of [DATE_TIME] and the Versailles Court of Appeal’s judgment of [DATE_TIME].

The applicant stated that he had lodged a complaint with the [PERSON] public prosecutor alleging arbitrary detention but had received no reply.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant made an application to the Indictment Division for his immediate release on the ground that he was being detained arbitrarily as the judge’s initial warrant of commitment had ceased to have any effect on [DATE_TIME].

In a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the Indictment Division dismissed that application for the following reason: “It is not disputed that the judgment of [DATE_TIME] was delivered within the time laid down by the last paragraph of Article 214 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Consequently, since the Indictment Division did not rule on the facts being investigated, the warrant of commitment issued by the investigating judge continued to have effect. …”

In the same judgment the Indictment Division ordered that the applicant should be kept in custody to avoid all risk of pressure being brought to bear on witnesses or collusion and because he could not provide sufficient sureties that he would appear for trial.

The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on grounds of appeal based, firstly, on an infringement of Article 725 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and, secondly, on a breach of Articles 201 and 214 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 5 of the Convention.

In a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal on the following grounds: “It appears from the impugned judgment and the documents on the file that on [DATE_TIME] a warrant of commitment was issued in respect of [the applicant], who was under investigation for offences including armed robbery. On expiry of its validity [DATE_TIME], the investigating judge extended the detention three times for [DATE_TIME], the final extension taking effect on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME], following the investigating judge’s transfer order of [DATE_TIME], the Indictment Division ordered further investigations. [The applicant] made an application to the Indictment Division for his release, alleging that the detention order had ceased to be valid on [DATE_TIME] and that he had been unlawfully detained since that date; that application was refused in the judgment now appealed against. In so ruling, the investigating court did not lay itself open to the objections raised. Since the judges ordered further investigations within the time allowed by Article 214, third paragraph, of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the initial warrant of commitment remained effective, in accordance with Article 181, second paragraph, of the Code, after the transfer order was issued and so remains until a decision on indictment is taken …”

On [DATE_TIME], after completion of the further investigations, the Indictment Division directed that the applicant be committed for trial at the Yvelines Assize Court charged with armed robbery, false imprisonment and other connected lesser offences. The judgment committing the applicant for trial at the Assize Court also contained an order for him to be remanded in custody. An appeal on points of law by the applicant against that judgment was dismissed by the Court of Cassation on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was tried at [LOCATION], which sentenced him to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment. In a judgment delivered on [DATE_TIME] on the civil claims the applicant was ordered to pay the civil party FRF 50,000 in damages.

In a judgment of [DATE_TIME] the Court of Cassation dismissed appeals on points of law by the applicant against the Assize Court’s judgments.

name: Thomas John Crompton
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 42509/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The parties requested an oral hearing, but the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant, Mr [PERSON] is a [NRP] national who was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION] The applicant joined the Territorial Army (“TA”) as a pay and accounts clerk, a military post, carrying out duties such as filing, photocopying and maintaining a stationery store. He was subsequently informed that the clerical post which he had occupied was to become a civilian post and was to be converted to that of a technical store-man. The applicant complained about redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal, but his claim was rejected. The matter was then placed before the Army Board. The Army Board, without holding an oral hearing or directing a Board of Inquiry to be convened, issued its decision on [DATE_TIME], refusing the applicant's claim for redress. The applicant applied for judicial review of the decision not to hold a hearing or convene a board of inquiry. The High Court granted the application and the case was dealt with expeditiously. The Board ordered that the applicant be offered compensation in respect of the failure to offer him alternative employment within the Army. It found in his favour as regards his argument that he ought to have been given priority. Army Board made a further compensation offer of GBP 94,016.67 to the applicant, which he rejected. The applicant, acting as a litigant in person, subsequently applied for judicial review of the decision, claiming that the award had not been properly assessed. The High Court accepted the Army Board's undertaking to review the level of the applicant's salary used in its calculation and, if appropriate, to reassess the award of compensation within [DATE_TIME]. Although formally the applicant was the unsuccessful party in the litigation, the court ordered the applicant to pay only half of the Army board's costs partly on the ground that “the history of this matter displays an inordinate period of delay”. The High Court has ruled that the applicant is entitled to compensation for the Army Board's failure to perform its duties. The Army Board awarded the applicant compensation of GBP 153,864.47. The High Court adjourned the case pending promulgation by the Army board of its written decision regarding the offer of compensation. The application was refused on the papers on [DATE_TIME]. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused. The case was adjourned pending the promulgation of the written decision. The applicant's application for judicial review was refused again on the ground that the decision had brought the finality he had been seeking.

The parties requested an oral hearing, but the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. The applicant is a British national who was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [ LOCATION], [LOCATION]. His claim was rejected because the Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over matters involving military personnel. The matter was then placed before the Army Board. The Army Board, without holding an oral hearing or directing a Board of Inquiry to be convened, issued its decision on [DATE_TIME], refusing the applicant's claim for redress. The applicant applied for judicial review of the decision. His application was granted by the High Court and the Army board was ordered to deal with the case expeditiously. It ordered that the applicant be offered compensation in respect of the failure to offer him alternative employment within the Army. Army Board made a further compensation offer of GBP 94,016.67. The sum was made up of three parts: loss of salary, redundancy payment and loss of pension rights. The applicant rejected the offer on the basis that it did not include costs or a sum to compensate him for the stress he had suffered. He subsequently applied for judicial review of the decision, claiming that the award had not been properly assessed. The High Court accepted the Army Board's undertaking to review the level of the [DATE_TIME] salary used in its calculation and, if appropriate, to reassess the award of compensation. Although formally the applicant was the unsuccessful party in the litigation, he would normally be required to pay the costs of the Army board. The High Court adjourned the case pending promulgation by the Army Board of its written decision regarding the offer of compensation. The applicant was represented by Levys Solicitors, a firm of solicitors based in [LOCATION]. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, [PERSON], Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

On [DATE_TIME] the acting President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3).

The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant, Mr [PERSON], is a [NRP] national who was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION], [LOCATION].

The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicant, may be summarised as follows.

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant joined the Territorial Army (“TA”) as a pay and accounts clerk, a military post, carrying out duties such as filing, photocopying and maintaining a stationery store. In [DATE_TIME] the applicant was informed that he was to be made redundant, following organisational changes in the TA pursuant to a process of civilianisation. He was subsequently informed that the clerical post which he had occupied was to become a civilian post and was to be converted to that of a technical store-man. The applicant applied for this new post, but was informed in [DATE_TIME] that he could take it only if he undertook a training course, but that all relevant training courses had been cancelled. He also applied for a number of other clerical posts within the Army but was refused for them all.

The applicant was therefore made redundant. His discharge from the Army, dated [DATE_TIME], was formally made, incorrectly, on the basis that his services were no longer required. The applicant later discovered that his former duties were being carried out by an untrained civilian, while the technical store-man post remained vacant.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant complained about his redundancy to the Industrial Tribunal, but his claim was rejected because the Industrial Tribunal did not have jurisdiction over matters involving military personnel.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant claimed redress in respect of his redundancy from his Commanding Officer, under sections 180 and 181 of the Army Act [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the Commanding Officer issued a brief in which he concluded that the applicant had a weak case for redress. He further requested the Army Board of the Defence Council to determine whether the applicant was subject to military law. The applicant's solicitors, on [DATE_TIME], submitted observations in reply. The matter was then placed before the Army Board.

In [DATE_TIME], the applicant applied for judicial review in respect of the Army Board's failure to determine the case within a reasonable time. His application was granted by the High Court on [DATE_TIME] and the Army Board was ordered to deal with the case expeditiously.

The Army Board, without holding an oral hearing or directing a Board of Inquiry to be convened, issued its decision on [DATE_TIME], refusing the applicant's claim for redress.

The applicant applied for judicial review of the decision not to hold an oral hearing or convene a Board of Inquiry.

On [DATE_TIME], while the judicial review application was pending, the Army Board directed that a Board of Inquiry should be convened. The Board was convened by an order dated [DATE_TIME]. It sat in [DATE_TIME], considered oral and documentary evidence and issued a summary of its factual findings on [DATE_TIME]. It found in the applicant's favour as regards his argument that he ought to have been, but was not, given priority before five selection boards. It was anticipated that the level of compensation would be fixed by negotiation between the Army Board and the applicant.

The Army Board met to reach a determination on [DATE_TIME]. It issued its decision on [DATE_TIME], ordering that the applicant be offered compensation in respect of the failure to offer him alternative employment within the Army. On [DATE_TIME], an award of compensation was notified to the applicant but he disputed the calculation of the compensation.

In [DATE_TIME] a further offer of settlement was made to the applicant, which he rejected.

On [DATE_TIME] the Army Board made a further compensation offer of GBP 94,016.67. The sum was made up of three parts: loss of salary (minus the applicant's actual earnings during the relevant period); a redundancy payment estimated on the basis that the applicant would have had [DATE_TIME] service; and loss of pension rights, again based on a [DATE_TIME] period. The applicant rejected the offer on the basis that it did not include costs or a sum to compensate him for the stress he had suffered.

The applicant, acting as a litigant in person, subsequently applied for judicial review of the decision, claiming that the award had not been properly assessed. Permission was granted on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant advanced two criticisms: first, that the award was based on the assumption that he would have been discharged from the army [DATE_TIME] after the date on which he was actually discharged; second, that the salary base used for the calculation of all three elements of the award was taken to be GBP 15,800 per year gross. The latter criticism was only formally advanced at the hearing itself.

On [DATE_TIME] the High Court rejected the applicant's complaint regarding the [DATE_TIME] cut-off date. However, in light of evidence produced to the court regarding the level of the applicant's salary at the time of his redundancy, the court accepted the Army Board's undertaking to review the level of the [DATE_TIME] salary used in its calculation and, if appropriate, to reassess the award of compensation within [DATE_TIME]. Although formally the applicant was the unsuccessful party in the litigation, and as a result would normally be required to pay the costs of the Army Board, the court ordered the applicant to pay only half of the Army Board's costs partly on the ground that “the history of this matter displays an inordinate period of delay”.

On [DATE_TIME], a revised offer of GBP 147,682.42 was made to the applicant. The offer was rejected.

The applicant again applied for judicial review on [DATE_TIME] seeking an order requiring the Army Board to investigate and take steps towards redressing his complaint within a prescribed time-frame and damages for the losses suffered by him as a result of the Army Board's failure to perform its duties. There was a hearing on [DATE_TIME] but no order was made.

On [DATE_TIME], a further offer was made to the applicant in the sum of GBP 153,000.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant again applied for judicial review in respect of the delay but again, following a hearing on [DATE_TIME], no order was made.

On [DATE_TIME], following another application for judicial review, the High Court adjourned the case pending promulgation by the Army Board of its written decision regarding the offer of compensation.

On [DATE_TIME] the Army Board issued its decision awarding the applicant compensation of GBP 153,864.47.

The applicant's application for judicial review was refused on [DATE_TIME] on the ground that the Army Board's decision had brought the finality which the applicant had been seeking.

The applicant brought a fresh application for judicial review on the ground that the award of [DATE_TIME] had been incorrectly reached. The application was refused on the papers on [DATE_TIME]. Following the applicant's renewed application and an oral hearing, permission was finally refused on [DATE_TIME].

The application was brought by two [NRP] nationals on [DATE_TIME]. The first applicant was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment. The second applicant already had three children from other relationships. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application. test_texts:
PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 44362/04) against [LOCATION] [LOCATION] and [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two [NRP] nationals, [PERSON] and [PERSON] (“the applicants”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicants, who were granted legal aid, were represented by Mr [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicants were born in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME], respectively. The first applicant is in prison (Dovergate Prison, [PERSON]) and the second applicant lives in [LOCATION].

In [DATE_TIME] the first applicant was convicted of murder and sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff of [DATE_TIME]. He is imprisoned in a private prison and his earliest expected release date is [DATE_TIME]. He has no children.

In [DATE_TIME] he met the second applicant, while she was also imprisoned, by correspondence through a prison pen pal network. She has since been released, although it is not clear when. In [DATE_TIME] the applicants married. The second applicant already had three children from other relationships.

Since the applicants wished to have a child, in [DATE_TIME] the first applicant applied for facilities for artificial insemination. In [DATE_TIME] the second applicant joined this application. Their solicitors made representations to the Secretary of State, relying on the length of the relationship and the fact that, given the first applicant’s earliest release date and the second applicant’s age, it was unlikely that the applicants would be able to have a child together without the use of artificial insemination facilities.

In a letter dated [DATE_TIME] the Secretary of State refused their application. He first set out his general policy (“the policy”): “Requests for artificial insemination by prisoners are carefully considered on individual merit and will only be granted in exceptional circumstances. In reaching decisions particular attention is given to the following general considerations:

whether the provision of AI facilities is the only means by which conception is likely to occur

whether the prisoner’s expected day of release is neither so near that delay would not be excessive nor so distant that he/she would be unable to assume the responsibilities of a parent

whether both parties want the procedure and the medical authorities both inside and outside the prison are satisfied that the couple are medically fit to proceed with AI

whether the couple were in a well established and stable relationship prior to imprisonment which is likely to subsist after the prisoner’s release

whether there is any evidence to suggest that the couple’s domestic circumstances and the arrangements for the welfare of the child are satisfactory, including the length of time for which the child might expect to be without a father or mother

whether having regard to the prisoner’s history, antecedents and other relevant factors there is evidence to suggest that it would not be in the public interest to provide artificial insemination facilities in a particular case.” He then gave his reasons for refusal in the present case. On the one hand, the second applicant would be [DATE_TIME] at the earliest possible date of release of the first applicant so that the likelihood of her being able to conceive naturally was small. Both applicants were also in full agreement about their wish to conceive artificially. However, on the other hand, and in the first place, the relationship was established while they were in prison and had not been tested in the normal environment of daily life. Secondly, there was insufficient provision in place to provide independently for the material welfare of any child which might be conceived. Thirdly, there was little in the way of an immediate support network in place for the mother and any child which might be conceived. Fourthly, any child would be without a father for an important part of [DATE_TIME]. Fifthly, in light of the violence of the first applicant’s crime, there would be legitimate public concern that the punitive and deterrent elements of his sentence of imprisonment were being circumvented if he were allowed to father a child by artificial insemination.

The applicants sought leave to apply for judicial review of the Secretary of State’s decision. On [DATE_TIME] the High Court refused leave on the papers. The applicants renewed their application and on [DATE_TIME] leave was again refused after an oral hearing. On [DATE_TIME] the applicants introduced an application to this Court and it was declared inadmissible in [DATE_TIME] on the basis that they had failed to exhaust domestic remedies (App. No. 34127/03). The applicants then applied to the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal.

On [DATE_TIME] their application was unanimously rejected by the Court of Appeal. [PERSON] relied in principle on the judgment of the Court of Appeal in R (Mellor) v Secretary of State for the Home Department ([[DATE_TIME]] 3 WLR 533). He pointed to the similarity of the arguments put by the applicants in the present case and in the [PERSON] case. Auld LJ relied on the conclusion of Lord [PERSON] in the [PERSON] case (see “Relevant Domestic Law and Practice” below) and commented: “... Lord [PERSON] clearly had in mind, and he set it out in the course of his judgment, the provisions of Article 8.2 of the Convention setting out various matters that may justify interference with the right to respect for private and family life, including the protection of health or morals and the protection of the rights and freedom of others. It seems to me that concern, not only for the public attitude to the exercise by prisoners of certain rights in prison which they would take for granted outside, and concern for the rights of a putative child in the upbringing it would receive depending on the circumstances and the length of the imprisonment involved, are highly relevant circumstances for the purposes of Article 8.2... Accordingly, in my view, it is not open to [the applicants] to seek to re-open the validity of the Secretary of State’s policy which this court has held in [PERSON] is rational and otherwise lawful. As Lord [PERSON] made clear in his judgment in that case, although the starting point of the policy is that deprivation of facilities for artificial insemination may prevent conception altogether, the finishing point is whether there are exceptional circumstances for not applying the policy ...” He then noted that on occasions the Secretary of State had “dis-applied the policy” when the circumstances had merited it: he referred to a letter from the Treasury Solicitor to the applicants which apparently demonstrated this fact and pointed out that counsel for the Secretary of State had informed the court that there had been other such instances.

[PERSON] then applied the policy to the present case: “To the extent that [the applicants have] suggested that he Secretary of State has irrationally misapplied his own policy to the circumstances, or has otherwise acted disproportionately in applying it, I would reject the suggestion. There is no basis for saying that the Secretary of State’s approach can be equated, as [the applicants] suggested, with the extinction of a fundamental right. It was a weighing of the starting point of the policy against the other considerations for which the policy itself provided, an exercise of discretion and proportionality in respect of which, in my view, the Secretary of State cannot be faulted on the circumstances as presented to him.”

The other judges also relied on the judgment in [PERSON]. Mance LJ said the following: “The case of [PERSON] is also clear authority that considerations and potential consequences of public interest over and above a narrow view of the requirements of good order and security in prison can play a role in a decision whether or not to permit such artificial insemination... I note that, in addition to the [NRP] authorities specifically mentioned in paragraph 42 by Lord [PERSON], the Commission, in its decision in Draper v the United Kingdom App No. 8186/78 at paragraphs 61 to 62, also recognised the potential relevance of more general considerations of public interest.”

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 47473/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant’s late father had applied to the Building Committee for tentative approval (förhandsbesked) of a plan to divide [LOCATION] and build a new one-family house. The purpose of such an approval, issued under Chapter 8, section 34, of the [DATE_TIME] Act, was to give a property owner who was planning a building project the possibility to obtain an advance assessment of whether the planned measures may be permitted at all, thereby avoiding unnecessary project work and costs. According to the detailed development plan in force, only one main building was allowed on the existing property plot. The father had wanted to build a house suited to his age, as he had difficulties in walking up and down the stairs of his current home. The applicant applied for a building permit. The Land Survey recommended that the property plan for Humanisten 1 be repealed in order to facilitate a division of the property enabling the applicant to construct a new house on the resulting new plot. The matter was at a standstill until [DATE_TIME] (see section 4 below). The applicant’s application was rejected and the Land Survey reported back to the Building Committee. The Building Committee granted a tentative approval to the applicant for a new one-family house. The County Administrative Board quashed the detailed development plan and the earlier refusal of a tentative Approval. The applicant then applied to the City Building Director for permission to build the new house. On [DATE_TIME] the Building Committee followed the Land Survey’s suggestion and repealed the property plan for [LOCATION]. The owners of two neighbouring properties appealed against the decision to the Board, claiming that the neighbourhood was worthy of preservation due to its special character and that new buildings would spoil the area. The Government quashed the Board's decision. The applicant applied to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) for judicial review under the Act on the Judicial Review of Certain Administrative Decisions (Lagen om rättsprövning av [PERSON] - hereinafter “the [Dates’] Act”) Supreme Administrative Court rules Government's decision was not unlawful. Court: Land may only be used for development if it is, from a public interest point of view, suitable for its purpose. The Government’s assessment that the suitability of the intended change of the property and the development conditions within the block ought to be reviewed through a new detailed development plan for the area, is within the scope of jurisdiction of the authorities in planning matters. The Supreme Administrative Court finds that the decision to quash the lower instances’ decisions regarding the property plan does not conflict with any legal rule in the manner claimed by the applicant. The applicant was given [DATE_TIME] to submit additional written observations. The application for a building permit was rejected by the Building Committee on [DATE_TIME]. The applicant appealed against the decision to the County Administrative Board, which upheld the decision. The applicant made a further appeal to the Government, which was rejected. A request by the applicant for re-opening of the case was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court. The matter was referred back for a new consideration. The application was later approved by the Office of the Town Architects for tentative approval. The neighbours of the applicant brought proceedings in [NRP] to have the measure quashed. They claimed that, although they were affected by the decision, the Committee had failed to hear them in the case or inform them about it. The Board quashed the Building Committee’s [DATE_TIME] decision on the grounds that the tentative approval was contrary to the existing property plan and detailed development plan. The applicant appealed against this decision to the County Administrative Court. In two separate decisions, the Administrative Court of Appeal refused the applicant leave to appeal in each case. In the second judgment it held that there no longer existed a tentative approval which was binding on the Building. Committee. The matter was referred back to the Board for further consideration. The Building Committee appealed against the above-mentioned decision of the Board. The application was rejected and the case was given priority. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court. The latter granted him numerous extensions until [DATE_TIME] of the time-limits for filing written submissions on the appeal concerning the building permit. The applicant requested the District Court (tingsrätten) of [PERSON] to declare that [LOCATION] was liable to pay him compensation for both actual and potential damage caused by the Municipality’s refusal to grant his request for a building permit despite having granted him an unconditional tentative approval which was binding. The District Court took note of the. Municipality's argument that the tentative approval was conditional upon an amendment to the property plan, and that the applicant was aware of the need to modify the. property plan. The District Court found that the Building Committee had disregarded a clear and unambiguous provision in the [DATE_TIME] Act, i.e. Chapter 8 section 34. The Court of Appeal (hovrätten) of [LOCATION] and Blekinge, upheld the lower court’s judgment in full. As no further appeal was lodged, the Court of appeal’S judgment acquired legal force on [Date_TIME].2. Request for compensation in an amount of SEK 3,000,000 for the damage he had suffered due to the refusal to grant him the building permit. He claimed that this damage corresponded to the market value of the part of his property upon which he would have built the house. The Supreme Court found that the applicant had not been able to demonstrate that the consideration of his application for a tentative approval by the Municipality of Lund, while blameworthy, had led to his being denied a definite right to divide and build a new house on his property. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Supreme Court, which on [DATE_TIME] refused the applicant leave to appeal. The. applicant had failed to show that a building permit granted by the. Municipality would have stood after the review by higher. instances. The Municipality could reasonably argue that the question of damage could not therefore be assessed only on the basis of the fact that the municipality was formally obliged to grant the applicant a building. permit.

The application was lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The applicant’s late father had applied on [DATE_TIME] to the Building Committee ([PERSON) of [PERSON] for tentative approval (förhandsbesked) of a plan to divide [LOCATION] and build a new one-family house. According to the detailed development plan in force, only one main building was allowed on the existing property plot. The Building Committee informed the applicant that he could not expect to be granted a building permit and therefore did not give tentative approval for the project. The new owner of the property appealed against both decisions to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) The applicant had applied for a tentative approval of a plan to divide the plot – Humanisten 1 – and to build a new one-family house. The Land Survey recommended that the property plan be repealed in order to facilitate a division of the property enabling the applicant to construct a new house on the resulting new plot. On [DATE_TIME] the Board agreed with the applicant, quashed the City Building Director’s decision to adopt the plan and remitted the matter to the Committee for a new examination. After the matter had been considered by the relevant road network and energy authorities, the applicant submitted new plans for the property. It appears that those proceedings were at a standstill until [Date_TIME) (see section 4 below) Neighbours of applicant's house oppose plan to build new buildings in their area. Government quashes the Board's decision to repeal the property plan for Humanisten 1. The Government find that the entire block has long been occupied by buildings in accordance with the city plan and plot divisions. The block has 10 plots, the sizes of which vary between approximately 750 m² and 1100 m². Government find the suitability of the intended change of the property and the development conditions within the block ought to be examined through a new detailed development plan for the area in which size and situation of the buildings can also be regulated to a sufficient extent. Supreme Administrative Court ruled that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. Supreme Administrative Court held that the decision to quash the lower instances’ decisions regarding the property plan does not conflict with any legal rule in the manner claimed by the applicant. The court held: “According to section 1, section 6, of the [[DATE_TIME] Act] land may only be used for development if it is, from a public interest point of view, suitable for its purpose. .... According to point 2 of the aforementioned provision, a detailed development plan becomes relevant when a new single building is to be constructed” The Supreme Administrative Court refused a request by the applicant for re-opening of the case. The applicant appealed against the decision to the Board, which upheld the Council’s decision. It found that the public interest in protecting the cultural heritage of the neighbourhood outweighed the applicant's private interest.
